Consideration in Committee of Bill No. 173, respecting British Nationality naturalization and aliens, Mr. Doherty-resumed from May 30; Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On new section 19-procedure and evidence in different provinces:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have given consideration to the observations made the other day in connection with the procedure that should be adopted. It was pointed out to ane that the provision with regard to what courts should deal with this matter in Hew Brunswick, being the provision reproduced from the old Act, was not suitable at the present day in view of changes that have been made in the constitution of the courts of that province. The observation of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car veil) I find on inquiry to be justified by the changes that have been made, and 1 therefore desire to move to amend subsection b of section 19 by substituting for the present provision:
In New Brunswick, to the circuit court in the county in which the alien resides or to the county court having jurisdiction in such county.
Subsection as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I -also desire to amend subsection h. I move that it be struck out and the following substituted:
In Saskatchewan and Alberta, to the Supreme Court sitting in the judicial district in which the alien resides or to the district court in such district.
That is to meet the objection that whereas in all other provinces this matter is submitted to the court, in Alberta and Saskatchewan, under the Act as first drafted, it was submitted to the judge who might sit in chambers. There were probably good reasons for that at the time the old law was enacted, as the courts were less numerous and sat less often in those provinces; but in the present condition of affairs there seems no good reason to continue a difference between those two provinces and the others.

I think the minister is in error in saying that the change in conditions in those provinces to-day rendered it unnecessary that there should be an opportunity of hearing these applications in chambers. Three years ago, although the area of territory was of the same size, the area occupied by population was much less. Now, with population scattered practically all over those provinces, the points at which courts sit naturally represent convenience for only a comparatively small part of the population. But there still remains a large part of the population who would be inconvenienced, and I think unnecessarily, if they were compelled to attend at the sit-

ings of the court. Unless there is some very serious reason I would very strongly urge that the matter be left as it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As the law stands they were bound to send these applications to the officers of the court and they had to be posted in the offices of the court. In that respect there is no substantial change, they still have to merely send their applications. The only difference is that instead, as under the old system, of these applications being forwarded on to the judge who dealt with them in chambers with no publicity and with no very easy opportunity for parties to be heard, we propose that in these provinces as in the other provinces the matter shall be dealt with by the court. The hon. member suggests that there will be difficulties about parties attending. I propose to amend section 21 so that the parties shall attend for examination except in cases where it is established to the satisfaction of the court or judge that there are good and sufficient causes preventing their being there. I think that with this combination we shall reduce to a minimum the inconvenience that will result, and we will have the advantage of not making differences between different provinces as to the tribunal which is to administer this law.

The Minister of Justice, by this Bill, is going to make it about as hard for a man of foreign nationality to become a British subject as for the ordinary common sinner to obtain a passport to to the kingdom of Heaven. If any one who knows anything about circuit courts, even in the eastern provinces, were to be told that if any special number of men, eight or nine or ten even, wanted to be naturalized they would have to go through the complicated procedure which my hon. friend prescribes; that they would have to attend on the opening day of the court and obtain counsel to consult with the judge as to whether their applications for naturalization can be considered, and upon what day; that they would have to wait until the criminal proceedings, which are usually the first initiated in any circuit court, are disposed of, he would consider the procedure impossible. My hon. friend is not inclined to trust the judgment of the judge to the extent of permitting him to hear these cases in chambers. It is impossible for one engaged in active practice to appreciate what my hon. friend means by all this even as regards eastern Canada, but when we consider that in the West whole colonies of aliens at a time want to obtain British citizenship, and that

under this Act these men are not to be given the opportunity of coming before a judge in chambers but have to depend on the sittings of the criminal court in the district, my hon. friend is simply intimating to every man of foreign blood in this country that he must not think of attempting to get British citizenship. My hon. friend will not allow a judge sitting in chambers to pass upon the evidence as to the man's qualifications. Counsel has to be employed . and all these technical difficulties overcome. Under these circumstances, I say that no man can be naturalized in this country in less than six months or a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as the hon. gentleman has dealt with the procedure before the courts, I would like to point out that there is no additional complication.
Oh yes, there is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the law stands at present in every province, excepting Alberta and Saskatchewan, the first thing a man has to do is to give notice to the clerk of the court of his intention to apply for naturalization. The clerk of the court has to post that for three weeks, and at the end of that time the court deals with the application. The difference that is made as to the tribunal is simply to assimilate the law of Alberta and Saskatchewan to that of the rest of the provinces. We are adding nothing to the complications or to the difficulties. The only other difference is this, that a man must make evidence to the satisfaction of the judge of the facts on which he relies, instead of 'as at present merely making an affidavit before a commissioner or a justice of the peace, which affidavit, if it satisfies the commissioner or justice of the peace, is sent to the court, which passes it. I have difficulty in seeing what is the great additional complication that is created. Under this Bill a man, instead of giving notice to the clerk of the court, sends his application to the clerk. Surely the one is no more difficult than the other. The application is dealt with just as the notice is dealt with under the law as it stands to-day, which prescribes that that application must be made in open court on the first day of the court. In this legislation we have not made that specific requirement. We have provided simply that the application shall be heard before the court three weeks after it has been filed with the clerk. Any man can now file his application by sending it by mail; and that,
with all respect, I think is a great improvement. The thing we do require is-that this matter shall be dealt with before the court and evidence given to the satisfaction of the judge, instead of the casebeing made to entirely rest upon an affidavit taken outside the court by an officer having, in the large majority of cases at all events, very little judicial qualifications. Under the present law he alone requires to be satisfied in the event of there being no opposition. I think the hon. member is unduly apprehensive of difficulties in this connection. As against such difficulties as' may arise, we have the protection resulting from the fact that these men coming forward to be naturalized will pass before the judge and will be subjected to examination. In that way we will have a guarantee of the genuineness of their application, and of the perfect truthfulness of what they say. I think the hon. member has experience enough to know that affidavits are not a satisfactory sort of proof of any fact that it is important to verify. Without casting any reflection upon the good faith of people that make-them, it is very possible that an affidavit may be erroneous or misleading, and there is much greater possibility of that when it comes to dealing with a class of people who are not perfectly familiar with the language in which these affidavits aTe drawn up. 'I must confess that I do not, see that w-e are making any additional' complications. I think that practically without additional complications we are getting a guarantee of the truthfulness of the statements on which the naturalization is granted.

Suppose a hundred
Galicians in a district in the Northwest desire to become naturalized-and that is e very small proportion of the- very large colonies in the Northwest-according to my hon. friend's difficult practice, those hundred men who want to become British subjects and who have complied with the residential regulations, must appear at court, and there will be a hundred applications entered upon the docket of the court sitting in that district. In that term of the court there will doubtless be criminal and civil cases to be heard at which the attendance of jurors and witnesses and all that is involved. My hon. friend undertakes to say to that judge who is sitting in term: You must not venture to take up this matter of naturalization in chambers; that will never do at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman realize that except in Alberta and Saskatchewan the judge cannot do it today?

Excepting in those
provinces we do not find an abnormal number of people applying at once for naturalization. Under my hon. friend's legislation these men, who may be of the working class, are kept hanging round the court until the judge permits them to present their cases. I am giving a case that has arisen and will he sure to arise again in the Northwest.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Are there terms in
Saskatchewan?
I am so advised.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Cannot the judge sit in court?	*
Not in our province, except by consent, and on the dates named.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He can in the city of
Halifax. When he is on circuit I think he can sit in court wherever he sees fit for certain purposes.

I have been in practice in my county for twenty-five years and I never remember any judge of the Supreme or county court attempting to sit out of term or not in accordance with the conditions imposed by the statute. I' fancy that in the Northwest provinces you would have that same condition. When the right hon. gentleman suggests that a judge could sit in term and try a particular case-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say sit in term; I said sit in court.
How is the foreignborn gentleman who lives some distance away from the court to know the time at which the judge may make up his mind to sit?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is a (very simple
remedy. When these applications are to be made, I suppose, they will be made by some person having a knowledge of )the law, and he will ask the judge to sit in court for the purpose of disposing of them. There may be provincial statutes permitting that to (be done.

The question of what a judge may or may not do is something which my right hon. friend knows very well is not a matter to be settled by the mere whim of Parliament or of the party who wants to be naturalized. I am deal-

ing with the ordinary conditions that must exist under the statute, and I am taking the case of, say, a hundred Galicians out in the Northwest who want to become naturalized. They know that according to the law of the land the judge will come to the chief town in their vicinity at a certain time. They proceed to give notice, the notice is given to the clerk of the court, it is posted and the term opened for the disposal of criminal and civil business, jury and nonjury cases. What is the judge going to do who sits in term, and who is compelled to sit in term, in these cases? There may be a man charged with murder, or there may be men charged with grave crimes awaiting trial, and, under these circumstances, is the judge going to say: They must stay here until I have gone into all these cases, heard the evidence of all the witnesses and reached the conclusion as to whether I shall issue a certificate or not? Is he going to do that as a matter of practice? No judge will do that. First, the judge will take up the criminal cases, then he will take up the civil jury cases, then he will take up the non-jury cases in which parties on both sides are interested and he will say to Mr. Galician:	You will have
to wait until these cases are disposed of, and the result is that the unfortunate man who wants to become a British citizen is told that he has to sit around the courthouse and pay for his board and all that sort of thing until the judge sees fit to take up these matters.
What would you suggest?
I would suggest that there should be no change in the law, that the judge should be permitted to take these matters up in chambers without waiting for the term of the court.

The objection I had to
section 19 was that in Alberta and Saskatchewan you can go before the judge in chambers while in other provinces you have to go to open court and that, whereas, in these provinces you are permitted to make your -case by affidavit, in other places you have to do it by viva voce evidence.

The remedy is to
permit a- party who wants to be naturalized to go before the judge in chambers after he has given notice anywhere in the Dominion. Why should he not? The judge is going to make a thorough investigation sitting in chambers without being hampered

by other parties and other proceedings, and he is going to give a certificate to he sent to the Secretary of State in quite as impartial a manner as if he were sitting in open court. The limitation is not only confined to Alberta and Saskatchewan biit in the east it is the same. Why should not Parliament trust a judge to hear these cases with the same fairness with his gown off as with his gown on more particularly as there is the extra check of requiring the judge to send the certificate to the Secretary of State? This law, instead of permitting and encouraging men to be British citizens, is going to throw every possible difficulty and impediment in their way.

This point was up the other day and at page 4698 of ' Hansard ' the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is reported as having said:
That suggestion is very deserving of consideration.
I do not think the minister has given it, as far as Nova Scotia is concerned, any consideration at all. I would like to know what the answer is to the argument put forward by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) on that point. I pointed out the other day that the reason we had to go to court before was that we got the certificate from the court naturalizing the applicant. We have to get the seal of the court on the order of the judge and it was therefore essential that the court should be sitting as a court. Now the judge	is	not to give us
an order at all, the seal of the court is not used, and it is not in any way essential that the court be sitting as a court. We have to present the facts to the judge, and he gives us a certificate signed by him. There is nothing to say that it shall be sealed, and why we should be obliged to wait until the court is sitting to get that certificate from a judge I do not understand. In the county of Cape Breton the convenient thing would be to allow the county court judge to deal with this matter, and, as he is empowered to deal with it in the court, why should he not be empowered to deal with it in chambers? Most of this business is done with us in the county court judge's court. I think the fact that the judge is sitting as a court does not give him any more capacity to deal with a mere finding of fact. I agree that the law should be continued as it is, with whatever other safeguards the minister wants to throw around it. When we get the certificate why should we not get it in the easiest, simplest and most convenient way?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry that my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) should think that I have not given sufficient consideration to what he said the other day. I can only deal with one thing at a time and express my opinion upon the representations which have been made to me one after the other. That is the reason why I have not reached the stage of giving to the hon. member who has just sat down the results of the serious consideration which I said his observations deserved, and which I have given to them. I must confess that the more I considered it the more I am convinced that much advantage will result from the fact that the question of establishing the qualification for naturalization is treated as other matters of importance are, and that is in a public, open court. There are many good reasons that lie behind the fundamental rule that the proceedings of a court must be public. Here, we are dealing with a matter that not only the man who wants to get naturalized is interested in, but one in which the country is also interested. I think it is of great advantage that the transaction should go on in open court where the public, who know the facts concerning the individual applying for naturalization, may be present and where the proceedings will be treated as a matter of importance. While I regret to differ from the hon. gentleman, the more consideration I have given to this matter the more firmly am I convinced that the court should deal with it. I am supported in that view 'by the past legislation. The legislation as it stands today required that, save in the exceptional case of provinces in which at that time it was considered that conditions differed from those of the more settled provinces, and therefore in which it was desirable that the matter should be dealt with in a different way. With all respect to the hon. member for Edmonton, I may say that it is from those provinces in particular that it has been most strongly urged that this change should be made. I have had representations from numbers of people, not speaking from any party point of view, that it was very desirable that this should be done, and that the evil which had to be guarded against there was, not too great difficulty in people people becoming naturalized, but too great facility in people becoming naturalized, without proper precaution.

So my hon. friend
swung the pendulum to the other extreme. If it was formerly pretty easy for a person to become naturalized, it is now going to

be almost impossible. Many people in this country are always preaching about what should be done in regard to this, that and the other question, just as in the old country you will find from the newspapers that the souls of a good many people are worried over the danger of western Canada becoming Americanized, whereas people on this side do not take the matter into consideration at all. A great many <rood people, quite as impractical, will dilate with long specious theories about the desirability of hedging round the rights of citizenship in this country with extra precautions. My hon. friend should realize that this is a practical question; that it is of no importance to Canada whether a judge sits with his gown on or off, when he has to determine, merely as a preliminary investigation, whether a man has resided in this country, can speak either English or French, and is not a criminal. My hon. friend, in the working out of this legislation, is going to prevent the ordinary man from getting naturalized at all. How is a judge going to dispose of a hundred applications in a term, when he cannot adjourn them to chambers and take them up, as he can now, on a reference? Many a county court judge, sitting as a referee in chambers in many cases where nobody but the parties and the witnesses hear anything about it, will determine whether a man shall lose everything he has in the world in a financial way, will settle rights of the most important character involving hundreds of thousands of dollars. All that can be done in chambers. The procedure of all the provinces permits it to be done. My hon. friend says that, when a man is ambitious td become a Canadian citizen, he must not be permitted to prove these simple facts in any other wray than in open court, after every possible barrier of a legal character has been put in front of him and at an expense which in some cases will be not only onerous but prohibitive. This is not a political question; it is a question of a common-sense working-out of a law; and those of us who have to do with active practice .at the bar, and who know how these things are dealt with in court, know that under such circumstances practically no one in the West will be able to get naturalized.

I wish to support what
the hon. member for Pictou has said with regard to the conditions in the West, and to say in reply to the minister, (although

it may seem over-assertiveness on my part, that while similarity of the law is no doubt desirable, yet, when there is serious dissimilarity of conditions, it is only reasonable that the law should be varied to meet those conditions. The law is for the people, not the people for the law. The conditions in those western provinces are to-day as they were five years ago, so far as accessibility to the procedure of courts is concerned by a large number of the people. The courts have been carried out to places where there were no courts -before, but the people have gone beyond that again. I believe there are moire people inconveniently situated !as regards the situation of the courts to-day than there were five years ago, because, although there are more courts, there are more people and they axe further scattered abroad. There is that condition prevailing especially in the two larger prairie provinces, which does not prevail anywhere else in- the Dominion, and I think it- is fair to take that into consideration.
The other feature has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Pictou, namely, that it is in those provinces where the largest number of naturalizations will necessarily take place. Therefore, what would be a minor inconvenience in one of the other provinces, becomes a major inconvenience in those provinces owing to the larger number of people affected. As to the actual working of the law, a man's application is sent in. That does not involve any difficulty. If the judge sees fit to deal with the application on affidavit, there is still no difficulty. But I take it that my hon. friend contemplates that the judge, in dealing with the application, shall take actual- evidence from the person. That may involve taking evidence also from neighbours of the person, who are familiar with his life and condition. Where the applicant and his witnesses may have to travel a distance of 50 or 100 miles in order to reach the court-and I want to assure the hon. minister that that is a very prevalent condition- it is a serious matter if there is delay that can reasonably be avoided after they have reached the court. The hon. member for Pictou has pointed out the difficulty of fitting in a large number of naturalization applications into the ordinary proceedings of the court. The hon. minister said dt was desirable to have personal evidence in open court, so that the neighbours and

acquaintances of the parties interested would have knowledge of the character of the evidence submitted; but I am dealing with the cases where the applicant is situated so far from the seat of the court that there is no possibility of the people living in the neighbourhood of the court having knowledge of the facts of the case. It is a matter of knowledge of the people in the locality in which the applicant resides, which knowledge is brought to the *court by the applicant and his witnesses, but it is not a mattter of knowledge of the people who live in the vicinity of the place where the court is held. I do not wish to press unduly; but I think in view of the statement made by the minister that he has received representations from people in those provinces advising practically the procedure that he now undertakes to provide, it is only fair that I should place before the country the facts as- I understand them, so that, whatever may occur, I certainly will not be responsible for not having brought the matter, as I understood it, fully to the attention of the minister and of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I understand the matter, there is no probability of delay from having these applications disposed of in a formal way. The Legislature of Saskatchewan or Alberta could make a slight amendment to the law, which would prevent such delay. My own view is that no undue obstacle should be placed in the way of any person desiring to become naturalized as a British subject in this country, but on the other hand naturalization should not be given on the penny-in-the-slot principle. There should be a certain formality about it, and the proceedings should be of a character to impress the person seeking naturalization with the fact that inquiry is being made and that an important matter is under consideration-no undue obstacle, but, on the other hand, a certain formality which should be impressive to the party.
Would the Prime Minister, for my own information, say what action taken by the local legislature would meet the case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Subject to the opinion of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who is more familiar with the matter than I am, an Act of the Legislature of Saskatchewan providing that judges may sit in court either generally or for this particular purpose, at any time and at any
place, would remove any possible difficulty. I think naturalization proceedings should be attended with the formality of the court and not carried on in the somewhat informal manner in which these matters are dealt with in chambers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the province of
Quebec-I would not say throughout the province or in every district, but certainly in the district of Montreal-the Legislature has enacted that it is always term. This makes it possible for the judge to sit as a court at any time. That is one method which would meet the objections that have been made to the requirement that the proceeding be before the court and not in Chambers. As the Prime Minister has suggested, it is only necessary for the
12 noon legislature to provide for certain additional terms, or to enable the judge to fix the time when he will sit in court and hear these cases. The performance of the duties of the judge of the court, as prescribed either by the law of this Dominion or other laws, is a matter to be regulated by the provincial authorities; and if there comes a considerable addition of work as a result of the present measure, I should anticipate that any provincial authority would make provision to meet the public convenience in that regard by providing additional terms or otherwise. While it is true there are more peo-' pie in the western provinces than there were, it is also true that the Dominion is being called upon to provide, and is providing, a very considerable number of additional judges. In the province of Saskatchewan, for instance, the year before last we provided for one additional judge, last year for four, and this year for four additional district court judges. These j adges will have jurisdiction, and the province has been divided into additional districts where these judges will sit. And we have provided for three additional high court judges in Alberta. If the population has increased, the number of judges also has increased. Under the law as it stood, while the judge in chambers could deal with these matters, he could deal with them only in the judicial district in which the alien to be naturalized resided. And he could not do it in more than one place in the district. So if the attendance of witnesses were made necessary those witnesses would have to attend at one particular place in the district. There was no provision for the judge to travel about to every man's

door to take his certificate. Under section 21, I propose to provide that the party shall attend before the judge for examination, unless it is established to his satisfaction that there are good and sufficient causes to prevent it. I have no doubt that any court would consider that a journey of a couple of hundred miles, if other satisfactory evidence were offered, would justify the non-attendance of the individual. No doubt, with the requirement that evidence be given in court., somebody wi'l have to go to court to give the evidence. But, so far as that requirement is concerned, I confess that the more I have considered the matter the more it does seem to me a most desirable thing that evidence should be so given, that it is a matter to be dealt with before the tribunal. I do not think it is disputable that as things stand to-day there must be large numbers of people who are naturalized who, without any perjury whatever on their part-I am not suggesting that-do not meet the requirements. We have been talking about the West. But take it in the big cities of the East. Men are naturalized upon their affidavits. As it happens, the larger proportion of people seeking naturalization are people new to the country, in many instances very unfamiliar with the language in which affidavits have to be drawn up, and still less familiar with the meaning of any term that the law may use which has special significance. Large numbers of people are . naturalized together and through the efforts of persons who take an interest in getting them naturalized, for one cause or another.
I do not suppose that I shall be making a revelation or shocking anybody when I say it does happen that more people are naturalized at the instance of persons interested in them-through the desire of obtaining the advantage of their votes or otherwise-after they become naturalized, than at the instance of the aliens themselves. The sole requirements of the present law are that each individual should make an affidavit before a commissioner or justice of the peace -whose connection with the case ends there and then-and that affidavit is simply taken to the court and left for three weeks, and when that time has gone by,-if nobody has made opposition, the judge is simply called upon to issue the certificate.
Without the attendance of the party?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the law stands at present, there is absolutely no requirement

of the attendance of the party. We propose to tequire that, under the new law, save where it is shown to be impossible.
Is it the idea that the judge shall see the applicant and make up his mind whether he is fit to be a citizen or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has not been suggested that the judge should make a physical examination to determine his qualifications. But under section 21 it is required that the party should attend for examination unless it is established to the court that there are good reasons why he should not. It has not seemed unreasonable to us to ask a man, where it is conveniently possible, to submit himself for examination. A judge is in a better position to decide as to the truthfulness of what a' man says if 'he [DOT]asks him questions than he is upon the mere production of a document. I have no doubt that the hon. member is lawyer enough to know just what an affidavit can be made to say without constituting perjury, though at the same time going quite beyond the limits of exact truthfulness.

Up to the present time the process of naturalization of aliens has been very simple. The person desiring naturalization made the affidavit and declaration prescribed by the statute; these were handed to the crown attorney or to the registrar of the high court and at the sitting of the Court of Sessions or of the High Court of Justice the certificate of the magistrate was read in open court. No objection being taken, that constituted naturalization of the alien. This simple and entirely inexpensive procedure has aided materially in the naturalization of desirable aliens. The hon. Minister of Justice is now establishing a court before which a man has to go to establish his right to be naturalized and this will entail on the alien who desires to be naturalized very considerable expense. Most aliens under these circumstances would deem it necessary to retain the services of a-solicitor and instead of obtaining naturalization, as they can now, at the cost of say one dollar at the outside, the expense entailed will be $15 or $20. It seems to me that the hon. member is going far beyond the requirements of necessity when he proposes to establish a tribunal before which these men must appear to demonstrate their rights to citizenship in Canada. What we desire in Canada is to get an additional population as rapidly as possible so long as it is composed of persons who are suit-

able eitizens. Foreigners are continually being naturalized throughout the western portion of the province of Ontario, particularly in the Niagara district. At every session of- the court large numbers are being naturalized and they become good citizens. I think that the passing of this Act, as outlined by the Minister of Justice will debar a large number of persons from 'becoming naturalized, because they will not go to the trouble which is thereby entailed upon them; at any rate, I apprehend that this provision will entail more expense than the necessities of the circumstance warrant.
Will there be any practical or necessary difference between the cost of application heard before the judge in chambers and the cost of application heard before the judge in court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only fee that I can think of will be a fee to the clerk for the service that he renders. We certainly will not providte for any additional expense simply because the matter conies before the court.

I have already referred
to the fact that this Bill, in providing undei subsection b of section 2 that the applicant shall have an adequate knowledge of either the English or the French language, appears to be in a measure discriminatory, apparently without intention, against the very principle which underlies our Canadian immigration policy. I was in Regina the other day, and having voiced in this House an objection to the narrowness of this section I was rather surprised to find that a petition had been presented to a large body of men meeting there in convention, on behalf of a German section of the population of Saskatchewan protesting against that provision on certain grounds. It is alleged that these people live in sections which are in the nature of colonies in parts of the country that are sparsely populated. Coming in families from portions of Germany or Austria and being in a new country, they frequently live far removed from neighbours and the only social intercourse they have is with themselves. Because ot the vast territory which is embraced in the West, in many cases these persons have no neighbours, or, indeed, no neighbourhood, for many, many miles, and are forced by the newness of conditions in the West to live within themselves and by themselves. It seems unfair that a section should be put in which would work a hardship to these persons, who are worthy citizens of this country and
who, through no desire to avoid learning the English language and through no desire to be particularly restrictive in respect of their own, are forced of necessity to have only one language, their own. Whether they be Germans or of any other race, I think it is extending the restrictions too far to prevent these people by this section from assuming through naturalization the full status and rights of Canadian citizenship.
What was the tenor of the petition to which my hon. friend has referred?
It protested against subsection b of section 2 of this Bill.
Was it from the Germans?

From the Germans of a certain section of the province of Saskatchewan to the Grand Lodge of British America which met in Regina last week. I happened to be on the floor of the convention room at the time and felt it my duty to rise from my seat to say that I had protested against this section on the floor of the House. I was not called upon to speak for these people, nor do I hold any brief for them. I simply voice the protest I saw made against the Act, which I felt it my duty to do as a British subject and as a Canadian who is anxious to see that all immigrants in this country shall live under such circumstances and be invested with such powers as will make Canadian citizens and British -subjects in the best possible manner and in the shortest possible time.
For instance those people may live in that district for twenty years bringing up their children, talking at their firesides the German language, hearing no English of any account and they are therefore unable, under that Act to naturalize themselves and become British subjects or to have a vote, although they are paying taxes, contributing to the revenues of the country, developing our western prairies. They are debarred from the right of the franchise as well as other rights which they might reasonably claim.

How many citizens
will you find whose children are not able to speak English?

I confine my remarks to conditions that apparently exist and which have been protested against in the West. I do not desire to be discourteous to my hon. friend in urging these objections, but

the petition complained that Germans an the West, in Saskatchewan and Alberta, who live together in colonies, are deprived, by that section of the Act, from becoming naturalized. ,	.
What is the conclusion of my hon. friend? Does he think that there should be no language test?

I do not know that I
have really formed an opinion upon it. I have not given the question proper study. I think there should be a language test but I do not see any objection, where we have hundreds of thousands of Germans in this country, all over the new provinces and in the old provinces, in business of all kinds, to extending this Act and making official, for the purposes of this Act, the German language.
Then you would extend it to all languages?
Very well, if the feeling of the House is that that would be a crime I would not share that opinion.
There is no language test in the existing Act and it is going all right.

But there is in this Act. I do not know why any test should be put in here particularly, and I must confess that I am not in a position from that point of view to criticise the minister, because I have not given it any study. I merely rose to voice a protest that I saw in writing.
I protested against this very section on the same ground on the second reading.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to extending the
language qualifications so as to include other languages, I must confess that it seems to me to be exceedingly difficult to do that. Then we certainly would be open to the suggestion of discrimination. If it is desirable to have a language test, I submit that it is not possible to suggest that there is any discrimination because we prescribe the requirement that a person should be familiar with one or other of the two official languages of the country. If we begin to declare other languages official for this particular purpose, I do not know how we will be able /to draw the line without giving rise to justified complaints that any one language is preferred to another. This is not a matter of

preference but a matter of what is officially determined by the constitution. As to their being a language requirement at all, there are two things to be borne in mind. In the first place, so far as this is intended to produce an empire-wide naturalization, the requirement of the language test came originally from the home country and was acquiesced in by all the dominions and was so asquiesced in before this Government acquiesced. That in itself was a very strong reason why we should be willing to accept something that was so generally desired as a condition of arriving at a naturalization to be effective throughout the whole empire. From the point of view of our own Canadian naturalization laws, I quite appreciate that there may be instances where it may operate with some harshness in particular cases; but, after all, I would venture to hope that that is a passing condition of affairs. We are going to get together sometime I hope. 1 do not think that the communities the hon. member refers to desire to maintain themselves indefinitely as separate communities, speaking only the language of the countries from which they came. Unless they desire to segregate themselves, and I am sure they do not, the condition which may exist to-day is a condition that, with time, will improve and I would hope gradually disappear. I am not expressing any hope that these people should not preserve their language. My own idea is that the more languages a man knows the more man he is, and the better qualified he is to be a good citizen. I hope they will preserve their languages but at the same time I hope they will come to familiarize themselves, in the West more particularly, with the English language, but at all events with an official language of this country. That would be a great help in our getting together, and anything that does not work too harshly and may prove an incentive to our people to acquire language, one of the two recognized is, I think, a goode thing in the interests of our country.
After what the hon. member and some others said on the subject I gave the matter consideration and it has occurred to me that perhaps it would be fair, or at least would eliminate the suggestion of unfairness in this change if we added a clause to this law which would prevent absolutely its depriving any person who is in Canada before the coming into force of this Act of any right that he has to-day or at the time of the coming into force of the Act. I propose to add a clause to the Bill, when we come to

43i7
the end of it, making provision that every alien resident in Canada before or at the time of the coming into force of the Act, shall be entitled, if he chooses, to become naturalized under the present existing law, getting, of course, the naturalization that that law gives, -and for the purpose of enabling such persons to 'become naturalized under the existing law, the existing law shall continue in force for a period of three years after the coming into force of this Act, after which that existing law will stand repealed. So we will get this situation that as regards any man resident in Canada at the time this Act comes into force, he will remain absolutely with all the rights that the present legislation gives him to be entitled to be naturalized under that legislation, that naturalization of course, continuing as it is now, a naturalization effective in Canada only. In that way, every man in Canada before this Bill becomes law will be entitled to become a British subject in Canada just as he is to-day without regard to any language test and wdthout the five years' requirement* The new requirements will apply exclusively to people who come into Canada after the new law is in force. Nobody will have a condition imposed upon him after he comes into the country. In order that there could be any grievance in this change of the law, it would have to be assumed that the man came iinto the country counting on the existing law. Every man who does that will not be disappointed. Every man who comes in counting on the existing law will get the benefit of that existing law: but people who come in after this Act is in force will come in under the then existing law and will get the rights given by the then existing law. The practical result of that will be that nobody to-day resident in Canada will be asked for the language qualification provided he is satisfied with purely Canadian naturalization and obtains it within the three years following the coming into force of this Act; that is to say, in the period in which under the existing law he would be entitled to obtain naturalization. Those who come dn after this Act is in force will be the only ones to whom its provisions will apply, but they, on the other hand, will get as compensation for compliance with the conditions, in. some respects .more severe, a wider and more effective naturalization. I trust that this course on our part will be found at all
events to be evidence of a desire to absolutely avoid by this legislation depriving any man of any existing right, or of any opportunity he has to-day of later on acquiring any right. On the other hand,, it will start us with a law applying to those coming into the country in the future, which, with all respect to those who differ from me, will be a valuable law not only in so far as it is going to give a wider and more effective naturalization, but in so far as the conditions it prescribes will really be to the advantage of the incoming settler and the people of Canada as a whole. I think that anything that holds forth an incentive to the newcomers to this country to place themselves in a position where they may more easily come to appreciate and share the views of the people already in the country, is an immense advantage from the point of view of the welfare of this country; and after all this requirement that within a period of five years a man coming into this country should acquire sufficient knowledge of our language to be able to make himself understood in it and to understand it, is not a very severe requirement. I can understand that there may be difficulties in the particular conditions pointed out by the hon. member who spoke last, but surely we all hope that those are passing conditions. Every day that goes by helps to bring about a change in those conditions, and surely it is not a great deal to hope that within five years from the coming into force of this Act those conditions will be much less prevalent than they are to-day. I think we are perhaps asking a little sacrifice of the new man who is coming in, but on the other hand for that sacrifice he will reap an immense advantage for himself, and that sacrifice on his part will tend to further the common understanding between the peoples of this country and to place us in a position where our mutual understanding of each other will be at least very greatly facilitated. Surely a new man who is looking for naturalization and the privileges of a British subject, will realize that that comparatively trifling sacrifice on his part is not too high a price to pay, and I am satisfied that the country generally will reap a very great benefit from this requirement.

I regret that my hon. friend has not seen fit to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) as I think there is a good deal

in his contention. We are inviting Germans to this country; we are giving them free land in the West; we want these immigrants and there is no good reason so far as I can see why they should not be admitted to the rights of citizenship without a language test. The minister, to my mind, has not given any good reason for this very drastic change in a law which has worked out very well in the past and of which, so far as I know, there has been no abuse. To some extent I would be inclined to agree to an educational test. We want the voters of this country to be intelligent men who can decide on the questions that are submitted to the electors, and there might be a case for the proposal that an educated German should receive the rights of citizenship whereas the ignorant man unable to read or understand the language should not be entitled to those rights. I fail to see why we should pass a law that would exclude an educated German or Swede from the rights of citizenship in Canada just because he could not pass the language test, especially as they are coming in here by the thousand every year and many of them, especially the older ones, will never be able to comply with the statutory requirements in regard to language. If the minister must have some test, let it be an educational test rather than one of language.

Section agreed to.
On section 19-posting of application;

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So as to make the intention of the section more clear, I move that for the section as it now stands there be substituted the following:
The application shall be delivered at the office of the clerk or other proper officer of the court during office hours, and such application shall he posted by such clerk or other proper officer in a conspicuous place in his office for at least three weeks before the application is heard by the court.
The change is to make it clear that the application may be made by delivering it at the office.

(Translation.) I would
like to have from the minister an explanation regarding children born of Canadian parents in the United States. We have often considerable difficulty, especially at election times, in regard to such persons. Having returned to live in Canada, they claim all the rights of Canadian citizens,
and at certain polling places they are allowed to vote, while at others they are refused. I would like to know if this Bill makesi it clear whether or not these people have really the right to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
(Translation.) Children born under the conditions stated are really British subjects, and have a right to take part in all our elections, as fully as children iborn in Canada, provided that their father has not lost his nationality by naturalization in the United States. At present the law goes further, saying that even the grandchildren are British subjects, but by this bill that privilege is withdrawn. The law remains the same, however, with regard to children, provided their father is a British subject.
, Mr. BOULAY:	(Translation.) Can a
child born under these conditions come to Canada without being subject to the immigration laws'? That is to say, if he has not attained the age of 21 years, can he come into the country as a Canadian citizen, with all the privileges of a British subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
(Translation). The immigration laws are distinct from the present naturalization law. They make a distinction between the British subject and the Canadian citizen. Under them, to be a Canadian citizen one must not only be a British subject, but have resided in Canada a certain length of time.
On section 21-proof of qualification:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg to move that this section be struck out, and that the following be substituted:
The applicant shall produce to the court such evidence that he is qualified and fit to he naturalized under the provisions of this Act as the court may require and shall also personally appear before the court for examination unless it is established to the satisfaction of the court that he is prevented from so appearing by some good and sufficient cause.

In the event of his not being able to appear, what can the judge
do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Does 'unable' mean simply that he has to do something else? If it is simply that he has to do something else, the provision is of no use.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think that any court would decide that simply because a man for his own convenience wants to do something else it would exempt him from attending before the judge. The requirement is that it should be established to the satisfaction of the court that he is prevented by some good and sufficient cause, by something outside of his own action.
On section 22-order for naturalization:

Under the old Act there were forms provided for every step taken in the case, but there are no forms provided for here. It may be a question between the judge and the Secretary of State as to what shape this certificate shall take and that difficulty would be removed if there was a proper form of certificate to be put in by the judge which would be satisfactory to the Secretary of State.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It did not occur to me that there would be any judge who would not be able to write a decision that a man had the necessary qualifications which would be satisfactory to the Secretary of State. In dealing with the judge of a court, does the hon. gentleman think it is necessary for us to provide a form in order that he may be able to say in an intelligible way that a man had proved his case ? In section 24 there is a provision to enable the Governor in Council to make regulations about forms. I should think that, in so far as forms are necessary, the Governor in Council could be trusted to provide for them, but I did not think that it would be
necessary that we should hand the form to a judge. The certificate sent to the Secretary of State will be the judge's decision.

The judges have been-just as intelligent and capable during the last twenty years as they are to-day. I do not know about the judges with whom my hon. friend has had experience, but our experience is that a judge will not write anything for us. We have to hand him any orders that we want him to issue and if they are proper he will initial them. Under the old law, with judges quite as intelligent as they are to-day, a form was provided, and that is the form which the judge signs to-day. Before going to the court to-day to ask for an order of naturalization for a person entitled to be naturalized, you have the form copied from the statute book, which you hand in to the judge for his signature, and which then receives the seal of the court. Why should we not know exactly what would be acceptable to the Secretary of State so that we could present the order and get the judge to sign it. At all events it would be a universal form that would be used by judges all over the country.
I think the hon. gentleman is forgetting that this ;s an interim part of the procedure.

I 'quite jugiderstand
that.
It is something which will be settled by the judge having the papers before him, writing the word * granted ' on the application and signing his name.
That is quite right but you must present the proper form.
The Act provides for the form which must be brought before him.
But there is no special form.
Section 26 provides the form that the citizen subject will get. That is to be issued by the Secretary of State.

If there was a fixed
form then, my hon. friend, who is a practising barrister, could buy these forms just as he buys other forms and have them in his desk or among his papers and he would thus have the convenience of having a printed form to present to the judge. If every judge is to have his own idea of what the form should be there will be a great many forms in use.

Oil section 23-issue of certificate of naturalization by the Secretary of State:

I -wish to place on record any protest against any autocracy in this matter. This is a democratic country; it is a country in which we do not want any feudalism or overlordism or autocracy introduced that will in any way interfere with the freedom which we at present enjoy.
For my part I wisih to protest against such high-handed authority being given to any person. I have not the slightest reference to the hon. gentleman who is at present occupying the position of Secretary of State, but I do not want the power placed within the scope of any person to prevent perhaps hundreds of people from voting at an election, if they want to do so. The party in power might have a thousand people ready to exercise the franchise if the Secretary of State would issue tne certificates; but if the Secretary of State were advised that it was of advantage to his party to withhold the certificates for a week until the election was over, under this section he has the power to do so. I do not wish to have such temptation placed in the way of any one, and such an obstacle to the right of any man to exercise his franchise. If the Secretary of State is advised by some one in a constituency that it is of advantage to prevent fifty, sixty or a hundred people from voting by withholding their certificates, he can do so, and he is not bound to give any reason for his action; but he can just play fast and loose with the people, if he is inclined so to do. We cannot get saints or angels to become Secretaries of State, any more than we can get them to become other ministers, and I do not think any such power as this should he given to any man. I suppose this section of the Bill will pass, but I want to state my unqualified' objection to the giving of any such power.

I do not wish to obstruct the legislation; but the minister will remember that I moved that subsection 3 of section 2 be struck out, and my amendment was lost on division. In order to be consistent in regard to this legislation, I would make the same motion in connection with this section. I therefore move that section 23 be struck out.
Amendment negatived on division, and section agreed to.
