On motion of Mr. Doherty, Bill No. 213, to amend the Dominion Lands Act, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The object of this Bill is to make it possible for an alien, who, by reason of the passage of the Naturalization Act, will complete the period of holding a homestead before he becomes qualified for naturalization, to obtain bis homestead on declaring his intention to become a citizen as soon as he is qualified to do so. The wording of the section appears to lack clearness in some respects, and I beg to move that the section be amended so as to read as follows:
1. Notwithstanding anything in the Dominion Lands Act, chapter 20 of the Statutes of 1908, or any other statute, any alien who has not resided in the British dominions or been in the service of the Crown for a period necessary for naturalization shall be entitled to obtain letters patent for a homestead in the 304
same manner as if he were a British subject, provided that he satisfy the Minister of the Interior that in all respects save such period of residence or service he is qualified to be naturalized, and declare upon oath his intention to be so naturalized as soon as he has completed such period of residence or service.
I propose also a second section to read:
This Act shall come into operation on the first day of January, 1915.

On reading this Bill, I thought there was something lacking in it. The minister's amendment, it seems to me, covers the point I thought lacking in the original Bill. I will point out that by this Bill-a position we cannot avoid-we are doing something now entirely contrary to our original land policy. It was fundamental to our policy that no person should be given a title to a free homestead unless and until he became a British subject. Now we are foregoing that important provision. I recognize that something must be done- either we must be satisfied with the three years' residence for naturalization, or we must extend the requirements for a homestead, or give patent to a man who is not a homesteader. I would merely suggest that the looseness of the provision under which the man acquires the title to his homestead without being naturalized, as contained in the minister's amendment, is open to the same objections, if those objections are considered valid, as the naturalization law was under the former Act. And I would say, with all respect and without urging the matter too strongly, that I should think that the right to a free patent on the part of an alien should be made the subject of some more definite considerations than are contained in the amendment put before the House. The patent for the homestead is what the alien wants. That is why he is wi'ling to become a British subject-in order to get a patent. And when we give him a patent without requiring him to become a British subject, we remove a very large part of the consideration that would under ordinary circumstances induce him to complete his British citizenship. I think, perhaps, that side of the question has not been considered as fully with regard to its very great importance as bearing on the question of naturalization, as it should have been. I do not wish to delay the legislation or the House, but it is a very grave question if we are not losing as much by allowing a free homestead patent to issue to an alien as we are gaining in insisting on the five years' residence. In fact I am not sure that we are not losing more; I am afraid we are.'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This legislation is intended really to cover what must be a period of transition from the one system to the other. This provision, in view of the amendment which we made this morning to the Naturalization Act enabling everybody now in Canada to obtain naturalization under the old system, will apply only to persons coming in after the Naturalization Act was passed. For the first three years anybody who has been three years in the country-and this is necessary in order to enable him to get his patent-will be in a position to be naturalized under the . old Act. This legislation, therefore, will begin to have practical application only after the lapse of these three years and if its operation is found to be attended with objection, we will be able to remedy it without being subject to the suggestion that by this legislation we discouraged any one from coming into Canada. The argument that was made-and I must say that it carried weight with it

was that if we change this law absolutely and at once and leave standing the absolute requirement that a man must be a British subject we may in the future be open to the suggestion that people came in here under the belief that they could get their patents Mter three years' residence and that that belief was being disappointed by our action. That contingency, of course, has been obviated by the amendment to the Naturalization Act. But it was further suggested that if we said that everybody coming in in future must necessarily stay five years before they can get their patents, that might operate to discourage people from coming in and taking homesteads, and that it might be a lesser evil to allow a man from whom we required that he establish t-o the satisfaction of the Minister of the Interior that he has every qualification for naturalization excepting complete period of residence, upon his making oath that he intends to be naturalized as soon ae the period is completed, to take his homestead in the meantime. It seems to me that we might without .very great risk venture to give a trial to that system and if its operation discourages people from being naturalized, we will have to consider what should foe done. But in order to have that effect the desire of a homestead must operate so strongly that persons will be willing to take a false oath with regard to their intentions. I think that a man who comes to Canada and lives

here for three years, fulfilling all the requirements necessary to enable him to get his homestead, establishing that he is a man of good character and fully qualified to be naturalized, and adding his sworn declaration that he intends to reside here and become naturalized, is . one whose patents we might freely endorse and whom we might safely trust not to make a false oath with regard to his intentions in order to get his patent. As I say, however, the law will not come into practical effective operation for some little time and perhaps our experience between now and then may throw more light on the desirability of maintaining it in force. In the meantime it will serve the purpose that our Naturalization Act will not operate to discourage immigration merely upon the ground that a longer period of residence will be required before patent may be obtained.
I do not see quite clearly whether in fact a man who is now in the country must naturalize in order to get his patent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Must naturalize under the old system. This Act applies only to persons who have not resided in British dominions or been in the service of the Crown for the period necessary for naturalization. For the coming three years the only period necessary for naturalization will be the period of three years after which a man may become naturalized under the old system, so that no man to whom that case is open will meet the requirements of this provision.
He cannot get a patent unless he naturalizes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, because the minister would say to him: you are not a man who cannot be naturalized because you have not done the proper period; on the face of it you have done three years on your homestead and under the law as it stands you are entitled to become naturalized under the old system.

That is satisfactory so far as it goes. The minister says that naturalization is something that an alien naturally desires, that to withhold it from him is our privilege and our right, and that we are thereby compelling him to come up to a certain standard. That is one side of the question; the other side is this: that the alien, having come to our country for a certain definite and material advantage and having been able to achieve that advantage without rendering himself liable to the re-

sponsibilities of citizenship, is satisfied and does not want to render himself liable to those responsibilities. The idea of the Governments of former days-and I do not mean to say the Liberal Government particularly- was that in consideration of the materia] advantage that we were allowing the alien to acquire freely in our country, we must have his allegiance and citizenship and the full responsibilities of them. We furnish the one material side; 'he must furnish the other. 1 am sure that it is not necessary for the Government to await experience in regard to the matter. I am satisfied that the facts that have manifested themselves .from day to day during many years past, have justified the wisdom of former governments in making assumption of the full responsibilities of Canadian citizenship a condition of the requirement of free lands from the Canadian Government. It is not necessary to wait to try that question out, and, without any desire unduly to criticise, I take this opportunity of saying that the Government is not well advised in waiting for that experience. I am well assured that the experience will not be to the benefit of the country and that it will create a situation of difficulty for the Government that, I think, had better be avoided. I repeat that it would be better to hold this Bill until the questions that naturally and necessarily arise under it are considered more fully than they have been considered. I am sure that the consideration of this matter that has taken place in Parliament has brought to the mind of the minister points of view which did not occur to him in the original consideration of the question. I am sure that if the matter is held over he will see that this question is touched on so many points and from so many angles that it would be the part of wisdom to revise the Bill in many particulars before it becomes law. It will create confusion if it is put in force before the many different and interweaving results are understood.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I said, I quite
recognize that there is a great deal of force in what the hon. gentleman says *and it may also be said that since the Bill has been introduced the position has been altered by the amendment made this morning to the Naturalization Act. The effect of that legislation, of course, is to postpone the necessity of legislation of this kind because anybody who 'becomes qualified to get a patent during the next three years will also have become qualified to 3041
become naturalized under the old system; and it may therefore be a proper subject, for consideration whether the Bill might not be allowed to stand over. I would dike to consider the matter from this new point of view, and for that purpose I beg to move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Motion agreed to and progress reported.

Mr. DOHERTY moved.
That the Order of the House of this day that the Bill, No. 173, respecting British Nationality Naturalization and Aliens, be ordered for a third reading at the next sitting: of the House be discharged, and that the said Bill be now read a third time.

I desire to say a few
words in opposition to the third reading of this Bill. First, I think it ought not to be read a third time, it ought not to come into force, until we know what the Imperial Parliament is doing in the matter of naturalization. I am told that the Bill has not yet passed the Imperial Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Bill has passed the House of Lords and stands for third reading in the 'House of Commons. It has been passed as submitted without amendment in committee, and it is expected it will receive its third reading as soon as our Bill does. This Bill only comes into force on the 1st of January next so that if anything should happen to prevent the-passage of the Imperial Bill this would not come into force before we could deal with the matter if action is called for.

I have a copy of the
Imperial Bill and I notice that when at was introduced there was very strong criticism of some of its provisions, and the-Government promised to consider the representations which were made. One strong objection was taken in the Imperial House of Commons, which I also take to this Bill. That is with reference to the status of a woman who is a British subject. This Bill provides, as the Imperial Bill also provides, that the moment a woman who is a British subject marries an alien she thereby ceases to he a British subject and becomes an alien. As stated in the Imperial House of Commons, that is manifestly unfair to-the woman, and I think in these days when

the law recognizes that a married woman ought to have the same status as a married man, it is entirely wrong to provide that if she happens to marry an alien she thereby ceases to be a British subject, even although she continues to reside in the British Empire. This will be the position of the married woman the moment this Bill comes into effect; although the woman may continue to reside in Canada, the very moment she marries an alien she ceases to be a British subject, and when her husband dies she continues to be an alien.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the present law.

Suppose it is, we ought not to observe for all time the antediluvian laws that may have been in force many years ago. It used to be the law of this country that a married woman could not hold property, that when she died all her personal property went to her hsuband, that her children had no right whatever in her property. All that has been changed, and from time to time Parliament has recognized that the status of a married woman ought to !be improved, and in most other respects that status has been improved. But it remains for this oanadian Parliament to declare in the year 1914 that if a widow, born a British subject, who may have children by her first husband who are British subjects, shall lose her status as a British subject the moment she marries an alien. Her children by the former husband, if he was a British subject, are British subjects and remain so, but she loses her status as a British subject and thereby becomes an alien; and even when her second husband dies her British citizenship is not restored to her. I submit that is not proper legislation. I submit it was properly criticised in the Imperial House of Commons when the Government promised to consider the representations and criticism made, and it is a provision which ought not to be passed.
There is another objection. This Bill is an Act respecting British nationality, naturalization and aliens, and yet it deals with the right to hold property in different provinces. I do not see what right this Parliament has to declare that an alien shall have the same right to hold property in the different provinces of Canada as a British subject. That is a matter which, in my judgment, pertains to the legislatures of the different provinces to deal with. Under the British North America Act, the provincial legislatures and they alone have

the power to deal with civil rights. Under the British North America Act, it is true that this Parliament has the right to deal with naturalization and aliens. That is by section 91. But by section 92, property and civil rights are placed among the subjects which are vested exclusively in the provincial legislatures.
I do not think there can be any doubt that in the provincial legislatures and in them alone is vested by the British North America Act the right to declare as to who shall and shall not hold property, and that this Parliament has no right to fake away from the legislatures of the various provinces of Canada the exclusive power which is vested in them under the terms of the British North America Act. It may well be that the legislatures of the different provinces may take an entirely different view, and that they may desire to declare that no one excepting a British subject shall be entitled to hold property within the province. Yet if this legislation passes, if it has the authority of law-which I hold it would not have-it would deprive the legislatures of the different provinces of the right to declare as to whether or not a person holding real estate must be a British subject. The question of the right to hold property has nothing whatever to do with naturalization. There is inserted in this Bill a section which is entirely foreign to the question of naturalization, declaring that aliens shall have the right to hold property within the different provinces. What has that to do with naturalization? I take it that the clause in the British North America Act providing that naturalization of aliens shall be within the powers of the Canadian Parliament, means as to the mode by which aliens may become naturalized, and that that is all it does mean. Under the British North America Act the exclusive right to legislate >as to civil rights is vested in the provincial legislatures. The Minister of Justice may say that we are simply reinserting a clause which was in the previous statute dealing with this subject. I am not quite sure whether the language is exactly the same or not, but I am rather inclined to think it is. Is there any reason for having it continued in this statute? We know that shortly after Confederation statesmen in charge of the affairs of this country held a very different view as to the powers of this Parliament and the legislatures of the different provinces from the views we are now compelled to hold as the result of the litigation which has taken place and the deci-

sions given by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The powers of the provincial legislatures have been enlarged by the court far beyond what many public men considered that the British North America Act provided. It does seem to me that if there is one thing clear as a result of the decisions which [DOT]have been given from time to time, it is that the exclusive right to declare as to who shall or shall not have the right to hold property in this Dominion belongs to the legislatures of the different provinces, and that this Parliament has no right to declare that an alien shall be entitled to hold real estate just the same as a British subject may hold it. I have a strong objection to this provision of the Bill, and I do not think it should be inserted. When we are dealing simply with the subject of naturalization, this Parliament ought not to declare, no matter what it may have declared in the past, that aliens shall be entitled to hold real estate in the provinces the same as naturalized British subjects. That is a matter which Parliament ought to leave to the legislatures of the different provinces. I had not an opportunity of being present when this Bill was being discussed in committee, and I felt it my duty on this occasion to express the views I hold in reference to the two points I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I need not say that any expression of opinion on a question of law falling from the lips of the hon. member for St. John has my most profound respect. I may say, however, that I did not introduce this Bill without giving consideration to all its clauses, including the particular clauses that have been referred to. As regards the hon. member's first suggestion that we should modify our law and make a new departure involving the creation of a situation where a married man and his wife would have different nationalities, I confess I do not see any call for legislation of that kind. I recognize that the hon. member for St. John does not consider that because things are old they are venerable, but still we have all been taught to admire the lady in the Scriptures who declared that 'Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.' I do not think there is any wrong done to a woman who, when she consents to marry an individual, is asked to accept his nationality. Whatever may be the conditions in the old country, I think I am safe in saying that there is no demand
in this country on behalf of the women for a change in the law in that respect. As regards the second objection, namely, that we are going beyond the scope of our legislative competency or jurisdiction in providing as to what capacity aliens [DOT]shall have as to the holding of property, I do not find it possible to accept the view of the hon. member. Although I do not pretend that it is conclusive, there is this to be said in support of the view that we have power to determine the capacity of aliens, that that view has been accepted ever since the British North America Act and there has been upon our statute-book ever since 1870 a provision not in the identical words but exactly the same in substance.

Does my hon. friend
know whether this question has come up in the courts at all? I am not quite sure- the Minister of Marine will probably know whether I am right or not-but I think the Legislature of New Brunswick has dealt with this very subject of aliens holding property.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No doubt that is correct. I cannot speak positively but I did ask the Deputy Minister of Justice and I understood from him that the question had arisen and had been decided. I shall be glad to look it up and if I find a case will communicate it to the hon. member. But even in the absence of a decision in the question there is enough within the express terms of the British North America Act to make it quite clear that the power is with us. In the first place we have the general power conferred by the British North America Act and the enumeration of subjects that is contained in section 91 of that Act is not intended to limit these general powers at all. The enumeration is only there to make it beyond all possible doubt that these subjects are included within the general terms of that clause that gives this Parliament power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces. The enumeration is only for greater certainty, but does not limit our powers. It is quite true that in the enumeration of subjects placed within the legislative competency of legislatures is property and civil rights within the provinces.
Exclusively?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Exclusively. What is involved in the question whether an alien may hold real property? It involves the [DOT]question of the capacity of the alien; it involves also the question of the control of property and civil rights within the provinces. And what is the provision of the law governing such a situation? It is to be found in the closing paragraph of section 91:
And any matter coming within any of the [DOT]classes of subjects enumerated in this section shall not be deemed to come within the class [DOT]of matters of a local or private nature comprised in the enumeration of the classes of subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.
When you come to have a situation where a certain matter, looked at from one side, is within the legislative competency of this Parliament and, looked at from the other, is within the legislative 'competency of the province, I take it that this section makes it clear that by the mere fact that it does come within this enumeration it shall not be deemed to come within the enumeration of powers attributed to the legislature. We are given control over aliens apd naturalization. I have difficulty in seeing how that [DOT]can be interpreted as meaning that we can only deal with the naturalization of aliens. The Parliament that enacted this law dealt with these two things as two distinct things. The same suggestion has been made in regard to the power that is given to this Parliament over marriage and divorce and it has been urged that this right meant that we had power over marriage only as far as divorce was concerned. That is an idea that has not succeeded in making its way and being recognized, and the evidence of it is that this Parliament has legislated with regard to serious questions raised concerning marriage absolutely unconnected with divorce. I entirely fail to see why we should assume that when an Act gives us control over two subject matters we only have control over one iij its relation to the other. If we have power to legislate in regard to aliens, and if legislation can be enacted in regard to aliens outside of making provision for their ceasing to be aliens, what legislation can we enact in regard to aliens as such if we are not allowed to say one word about their capacity?
This Parliament has exclusive power to deal with banks. Would the hon. gentleman suggest that because the provinces have power to deal with property and civil rights within the provinces, we cannot confer
[Mr. Pugsley.j
upon a bank which we have created the power to hold property in a province? In dealing with other matters entirely within the competence of this Parliament we necessarily deal with the question of property and civil rights in the province. When we incorporate a railway company we give it powers of expropriation. Surely there is no legislation more directly affecting the question of property and civil rights in the province and yet that legislation is not questioned. There are judgments holding that our power goes so far that, because the subject matter of the railway company is within our legislative jurisdiction, we can give it power to expropriate even the property of the province. There are numerous subjects just like this subject of aliens confided to us that you cannot deal with unless you touch the question of property and civil rights in the province. Take, for instance, the subject of bankruptcy and insolvency; there are numerous decisions upholding legislation affecting property and civil rights in the provinces because these Acts are incidental to the question of bankruptcy.
I think the suggestion in reference to provincial rights comes from a misapprehension of what is meant by dealing with aliens and giving capacity to aliens. It does not at all mean that because a man is an alien the province cannot look at the question from some other point of view and pass legislation in regard to his capacity. For instance, our enactment that aliens can hold property in the same way as British subjects goes no farther than to say that the fact alone that the man is an alien does not render him incapable but it does not go so far as to say that, if the province thinks it desirable that a class of persons who are aliens but who, besides being aliens, are of some particular class, should be excluded from the right to hold property in the province because t-hey were of that particular class it cannot so legislate. For instance, the fact that we say that an alien shall have the same power to hold property as a British subject, does not prevent the legislature, if it thought proper to do so, from saying that no coloured man shall hold real property. That coloured man would not be entitled to come forward, simply because in addition to being a coloured man he was an alien, and say, although you have legislated against a coloured man holding property, because I am an alien, I have the right to hold it. There you have thA

exercise of the right of the province to g( verr. the right of everybody within it to hold real property. The only restriction you attach to it is that they shall not say that purely and simply, because a man is an alien, he shall not hold property. But they are not precluded from dealing in any way they like with the property of people who are aliens. All we declare is that an alien shall have the same right to hold property as a British subject. Every British subject holds property in the province subject to the legislative authority of the province to say what particular classes shall hold property and our legislation does not give to the alien any mort right than the British subject but it simply puts him in the province just as absolutely under the 'Control of the province as is the British subject. It precludes the province from saying explicitly that because an individual is an alien he shall not have the right to hold- property. Unless the hon. gentleman is prepared to stand behind the proposition that we can give no right to hold property to a bank or a railway company or to any other company that we create, although the property may be absolutely necessary to its purposes, I fail to see how he can sustain his contention that we have no right to deal with the subject of aliens and that we have no right to say what their capacity shall be in so far as simply that they are aliens. The only effect upon the province is that the alien stands subject to their laws in the same way that the British subject does and they can make such laws as they deem proper with regard to his right to hold real property, to the same extent as they can with regard to Britsh subjects. The only thing they cannot do is to step in and deal specifically' with the capacity of the alien as an alien. Every British subject is under the control of the provincial legislature as regardsi property and civil rights in the province and under our provision so is every alien.

The minister has referred to legislation in regard to the building Of railways and in regard to insolvency, but I think he will agree with me that the right to take property by expropriation for the building of railways, and also the right to deal with property in the case of bankruptcy and insolvency, is necessarily incident to the subject with which Parliament was dealing in those instances.
In the case of railways, the Judicial Committee, when the question came before them, put the right to take property by expropriation entirely upon this ground that it would not be possible to carry out the intention of Parliament unless power was given to expropriate. Therefore it was necessary or reasonably incidental to the legislation upon the subject of railways. But it can hardly be necessary or incidental to this legislation dealing with aliens, that Parliament should have the power to say that an alien shall have the same rights in all the provinces of Canada to hold real and personal property of every description in the same manner as a British subject. I do not see that it is reasonable or incidental to legislation upon this subject at all. Section 17 of this Bill provides that:
Real and personal property of every description may be taken, acquired, held and disposed of by an alien in the same manner in all respects as by a natural-born British subject, and a title to real and personal property of every description may be derived through, from or in succession to an alien in the same manner in all respects as through, from or in succession to a natural-born British subject.
I am not able to agree with the minister that, even if this section should become law, a provincial legislature could determine that certain classes of aliens should not be allowed to hold real estate. If Parliament has the right to declare that all aliens shall have the right to hold real and personal property and to derive title to it in the same manner in all respects as a British subject, it seems to me it will take away absolutely the right of a provincial legislature to declare whether or not aliens generally or any class of aliens should be entitled to hold real or personal property. I cannot help thinking that it interferes with section 92 of the British North America Act, which vests civil rights and the rights of property exclusively within the powers of the provincial legislatures.

When this Bill was under discussion in Committee of the Whole, I called the attention of the Minister of Justice to the abnormal powers given to the Secretary of State under subsections 2, 3 and 5 of section 2. Subsection 3 reads as follows:
The grant of a certificate of naturalization to any such alien shall be in the absolute discretion of the Secretary of State of Canada, and he may, with or without assigning any reason, give or withhold the certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision.
Subsection 5 reads in a similar way:

The Secretary of State of Canada may in any special case, if he thinks fit, grant a certificate of naturalization, although the four years' residence or five years' service has not Keen within the last eight years before the application.
In other words it is another part of the Bill we are providing for special machinery to determine who should and who should not be admitted to naturalization. We have given the courts of law the power to determine that question, and we have provided that the applicant must come before the court and give evidence of his character; that the judge may, if not satisfied with the proof placed before him, ask for further evidence, and that there may be a trial before the judge as to whether or not the applicant is a fit and proper person to be a British subject. The only qualification required is that the applicant shall be of good character. The moment he has satisfied the judge that he is of good character, he is qualified to become a British subject. The judge determines the question, and then the matter is not finally disposed of, but is referred to the Secretary of State who, purely arbitrarily, without giving any reasons, but simply of his own will, may or may not grant a certificate. Such a disposition is absolutely repugnant to the spirit of our institutions. We cannot see why an officer of the Government or a minister himself should.be given such arbitrary powers. The only reason given by my hon. friend in justification of the introduction of this section is that such legislation has been in force in Great Britain ever since there was a law of naturalization there. The law in this respect has been absolutely different in Canada. When we adopted the law of naturalization, we did not copy the British precedent. We did not provide that the Secretary of State should arbitrarily have the power which is given to the home office in Great Britain; but we provided that the decision of the judge should be final and should not be revised by any one. I have not heard that any complication has arisen; or that it has ever been felt that there was in Canada any necessity, as there appears to be in Great Britain, for the Secretary of State to be given such power as this. What may be the reason why in Great Britain such an arbitrary power should be given to a minister of the Crown is something upon which I have not been able to satisfy myself. Although I must say that my searches have not been very extensive, I have failed to find any reason why the Secretary of State in Great Britain should be given such an [Sir Wilfrid J,aurier 1
abnormal power. It is absolutely contrary to the spirit of our institution, when a judicial matter has been decided by a court of law, that any one should have the power over that court to nullify its 4 p.m. decision without giving any reason at all. If there is reason for such legislation, it must be that the Government of Great Britain have found it necessary, in order to avoid diplomatic complications to reserve that power. It is a matter of history that, during the thirties, forties and fifties of the last century, the conditions in Europe were very uncertain; that there were civil wars in many countries, and threats of war and insurrection in others. In Poland, Italy, Austria and other European countries, there were constantly political refugees seeking homes and shelter in Great Britain. It is a matter of history that many times the Government of Great Britain have had representations made to them by the diplomatic agents of foreign powers against the presence of a particular political refugee who was plotting in Great Britain to disturb the peace of the country from which he was banished. It is a matter of history that some of these men often sought naturalization and were naturalized; and it is possible to conceive that, under these circumstances, the foreign representative of one of those countries at the Court of St. James might have thought it advisable to ask the Home authorities that a political refugee from such country should not be admitted to naturalization. If that is not the object, it is impossible to conceive of one; but it is an abnormal power, as every one will admit. We have not thought it advisable in Canada to take that power so far; nothing has arisen to show that we have not acted wisely, and I repeat that no good reasons have been or can be adduced why, at this stage *when we are revising our naturalization law	with the very laudable purpose
of	extending	its	scope, we shouldput	such	an	abnormal power into
the hands of the Secretary of State. Suppose that three, or five, or ten, or twenty men are passed upon by the courts as fit for naturalization in any part of the Dominion, you give power to the Secretary of State, for any reason-for political let us suppose, and on the complaint or representation of anybody who may have given him advice-to annul the proceedings of the courts of law, to make useless the expense incurred by the men in their efforts to become Canadians, and to set aside all the rights pertaining thereto; the

Secretary of State may do so merely of his own will and without being accountable to anybody. In the course of the discussion the hon. minister stated, and stated quite properly, that we are anxious to extend naturalization, so that those who come to this country to make it their home should, as early as possible, have the advantages that we confer upon them in the enjoyment of our institutions, the primary condition of which is naturalization. But after having provided all the machinery by which they may acquire these rights, we then appoint some one with power to take those rights away from them. I do not wish to prolong the discussion, but the provision is so dangerous and so unusual that I beg to move:
That this Bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions that they have power to amend it by striking out subsections 3 and 5 of section 2.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to first
point out that this discretionary power is one of the five provisions which, at the Conference in 1911, it was decided were essential to legislation of this kind. That was agreed to by the conference at which the right hon. gentleman himself (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was present representing Canada. Mr. Churchill, for instance, repeats these conditions a number of times. At page 187 of the printed report he says:
The grant of nationality is in every case discretionary and this discretion should be exercised by those responsible in the area in which the applicant has spent the last twelve months.
That is repeated several times. For instance, at page 194 Sir John Simon says:
It is essential to the scheme which the Home Secretary has referred to, that the grant of an Imperial certificate should be a matter of discretion, and that that discretion should be exercised, not in all cases by the Home Government, of course, but by the authority which has the local opportunity of judging of the man's personal qualities and credentials during the last year of his five years. That seems to me to be essential to the scheme.
That is again repeated at pages 196 or 199 by Mr. Churchill, and stands in that fonn until it is finally agreed to by the conference as a whole.
Now, may I point out what seems to me a very good reason for the reservation of that discretion. It was a question then of making a law prescribing conditions for naturalization, which by a method to be subsequently devised, and which we have devised, was to be made similar in all
British possessions, including, of course, the home country. The requirements laid down as being the means without which a man was not to be entitled to this naturalization, were to apply to all the British possessions, but it was not intended to bind any to give naturalization even to those who met those requirements. The right hon. gentleman says the proposition is that the Secretary of State shall have power to override the decision of the courts. In saying that he misapprehends the purpose of the Bill. What the court does is to decide that the particular individual meets those requirements of this legislation of general application, without which he cannot be naturalized. But the court cannot go any further and declare that the party has a right to be naturalized. It still rests with the country, through its responsible	government-'after all, the
Secretary of State is only one of a government that is responsible for what he does

to determine whether or not it will grant to that individual his naturalization. If you take that clause out, then you create a situation where each one of the dominions will be absolutely bound, because a man meets certain requirements which are agreed to be essential, to give him naturalization, even though, for reasons outside of the possession of these particular qualifications, the government of that particular dominion or possession might consider that it was not in the public interest for that man or that class of men to be naturalized. In reality the idea was, as far as the dominions are concerned, to reserve to them freedom of action, even when a man met those requirements which the mother country and the dominions generally agreed were essential-but not necessarily sufficient- to fit a man for naturalization. The purpose is to keep within the hands of each of the dominions control even over people who may meet these requirements, to place these dominions in a position where they may be enabled, for reasons that they may consider sufficient, to declare that a person, though meeting these requirements, is not a desirable subject, in their judgment, and to exclude him. While it is true that the Secretary of State is not called upon to give reasons why he takes a certain course under this provision, it should be remembered that he always acts as a member of a responsible Government, and the circumstances under which he acts, if he does act in the exercise of that power,

will always be before the public either for condemnation or for approval. He will act upon his responsibility and the responsibility of the Government behind him, and I think that that is sufficient protection against arbitrary action on his part. As I look at it, this is a power that will seldom, if ever, be exercised; but it is a power held in reserve which may prove most invaluable to this country. I should look upon it as a matter for grave regret if this Parliament should put itself on record as of the opinion that a discretion which may properly be vested by the Parliament of the home country in the responsible advisors of His Majesty in the imperial Cabinet, should not, through lack of confidence, Qe vested in the responsible advisors whom His Majesty through 'his representatives in this country may call to his councils from time to time. It seems to me that we may take the very slight risk that is involved. I know it is quite easy to use words which make this look odious; it is easy to talk about it as being arbitrary and as being liable to be abused. It is quite true that the power may be abused, but, after all, we ought to have confidence enough in our men not to refuse them any power merely because it can be abused. As to its being arbitrarily exercised, permit me to point out that it will have to be exercised under the eye of the Parliament and of the public of Canada, who are anxious that no unnecessary obstruction shall be placed in the way of naturalization. I venture to say that it will be a very bold Secretary of State indeed who will take upon himself the exercising of this reserve power in any arbitrary way. This provision is here because it was agreed that it should be here. It was put in in order that all the dominions might realize that by this legislation they were not depriving themselves of the discretionary power to deal with any particular case as they might see fit. The home Government considers that the discretionary power is essential; that it should be held out as an additional protection to each one of the dominions against the suggestion that its liberty was in any way restricted and that by agreeing to this legislation it was compelled to grant naturalization to any particular individual. I think it is well for us to bear in mind that this clause was inserted in execution of an agreement in which the discretionary power of each one of the dominions was recognized as an essential part of the scheme, and that we may expose the whole scheme to failure simply by reason of our own dis-
trust of our own public men. The fact that we would by eliminating this clause leave the Government of the day absolutely powerless in respect of the granting of naturalization would not be compensation, in my judgment, for the loss that the country itself would sustain through its being deprived of this valuable reserve power, and if what has been so long sought for should be defeated simply by reason of our lack of confidence in our own public men.

Whereas His Majesty the King (hereinafter called 'the Government,') and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, (hereinafter called 'The Company,') entered into certain agreements which were confirmed by and set out in schedules to Statutes of Canada, viz.:

' And whereas the company alleges that the proceeds of such bonds so implemented have proved insufficient to pay the proportion of the cost of construction of the western division as hereinafter defined, which the company alleges the Government by said agreements and under said trust deed became bound to provide, and the company claims that the Government is obliged to pay without recourse three-fourths of the amount required to complete the mountain section as hereinafter defined ;
And whereas the Government does not admit such allegations or claims and has offered to refer the questions in dispute to the decision of the courts;
And whereas to enable the company to continue its works without delay the company has requested the Government by way of compromise and in full settlement as below mentioned to guarantee a further issue of bonds to the amount below mentioned ;
And whereas it is in the public interest that such guarantee should be authorized upon the terms and subject to the conditions hereinafter set out;
It is therefore resolved that it is expedient to provide as follows :
1.	Unless the context otherwise requires, 4 western division ' means that portion of the line of railway mentioned in clause 2 of the said agreement of the 29th of#July, 1903, extending from the city of Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean ; ' mountain section ' means that portion of the western division extending from the east bank of the Wolf river to the Pacific ocean ; 4 prairie section ' means the remaining portion of the western division ; 4 guaranteed securities ' means the bonds hereby authorized to be guaranteed.
2.	That upon the company establishing to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council that the moneys available therefor and the resources of the company are insufficient to enable the company to complete the western division and that any moneys necessary for that purpose over and above the proceeds of the guaranteed securities will be provided, His
Majesty on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, may, for the purpose of aiding the company to provide the balance required for the completion of the mountain section including the expenditures mentioned in the proviso to section 4 hereof, and upon and subject to the conditions hereinafter set out, guarantee payment of the principal and interest of an issue of bonds, to be made by the company for a principal amount sufficient in the opinion of the Governor in Council, to provide for the expenditures set out in said proviso, not exceeding $16,000,000, such bonds to be payable on the 1st day of January, 1962, and to bear interest at the rate of four per cent per annum payable half yearly.
3.	That the said bonds shall be secured by a deed or deeds of trust (hereinafter referred to as the 'new trust deed') made to a trustee or trustees to be named therein (herein referred to as 'the trustee') granting fixed and floating mortgages or charges upon the present and future undertakings and properties of the company of every kind, tolls and revenues, rights, franchises and powers, subject only to.
(a)	the mortgage and charges heretofore created and the securities heretofore or hereafter issued under existing trust deeds or mortgages securing same or under or by virtue of any existing statute of Canada;
(b)	Such priority in favour of other mortgages and charges hereafter created by the company as the Governor in Council may expressly approve of as being in the interests of the company and of Canada.
4.	The kind of securities to be guaranteed hereunder and the forms thereof, and the forms and terms of the new trust deed, and the trustee, and the times and manner of the issue of the guaranteed securities, and the disposition of the moneys to be raised thereon, by sale, pledge or otherwise, and the forms and manner of guarantee or guarantees shall be such as the Governor in Council approves and such terms, provisions and conditions as the Governor in Council may consider expedient or necessary shall be included in the new trust deed.
Provided that no part of said moneys shall be used other than for expenditure approved by or under the authority of the Governor in Council for three-rourths of cost of construction work as defined in the said trust deed of 10th June, 19^5, in respect of the mountain section, inclusive of all interest until completion of the mountain section on bonds heretofore or hereafter issued in respect of same under the deeds of trust by way of mortgage dated 10th June, 1905, and 15th March, 1905, set forth in schedules (A) and (B) to chapter 98 of the Statutes of Canada, 1905, and interest upon advances made in respect of the mountain section under the Grand Trunk Pacific Loan Act, 1913, and for interest upon the guaranteed securities until the expiration of three years from the date of completion of the western division as hereinafter fixed.

The said guarantee shall be deposited with the trustee, signed by the Minister of Finance or such officer as is designated by the Governor in Council, and upon being signed and deposited as aforesaid, His Majesty shall become liable as guarantor for the payment of principal and interest of the guaranteed securities according to the tenor thereof and the said payment shall form a charge upon the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and the guarantee so signed and deposited shall be conclusive evidence that the requirements of this Act respecting the guaranteed securities and the new trust deed

and all matters relating thereto, have been complied with.	t

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any moneys paid by His Majesty under any guarantee given hereunder shall be held to be paid in discharge of the liability of His Majesty, and not in discharge of the liability of the company, under the guaranteed securities, or under the new trust deed, and the moneys so paid shall be held to be still secured by the guaranteed securities and the new trust deed, and His Majesty shall be subrogated in and to all the rights of the holders of the guaranteed securities, the interest or the principal of which has been paid by His Majesty, and His Majesty shall, with respect to the moneys so paid, be in all respects, in the position of a security holder with respect to whose securities default shall have been made in payment to the extent of the moneys paid by His Majesty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
ment bad put forward, or if the company were disposed to accept that view as to the legal rights of both parties in the premises, then we would be prepared to consider an application by the company for further *assistance in carrying out the enterprise. We considered that only reasonable, for the reason that whatever might be the legal effect of the arrangement of 1905, it -was perfectly apparent that there was a distinct agreement by the contracts of 1903 and 1904 that the Government would guarantee the bonds of the company to the extent of three-quarters of the cost of the mountain section, whatever that might he, and that the Government would implement these bonds and pay tne interest on them for seven years without recourse. The company pointed out that, in case the matter should be referred to the courte, a delay of eighteen months or two years would be involved, and they represented to us-and we have no reason to doubt the truth and accuracy of their representations -that if aid were not forthcoming in the meantime, they would have to stop the work, the plant which had been gathered together would have to he disbanded, and that in the end the cost of completing the road would be very much greater than it otherwise would have been. After a great deal of negotiation, it was finally arranged that the Government should give a guarantee of bonds, not at three per cent but at four per cent, because in the meantime the rate of interest had considerably increased beyond that which prevailed in 1903 and 1904, When the agreement was first entered into. It was provided that the Government should not be called upon to implement those bonds, that is, to make good the difference between the realized value and the par value, and that the Government should not be called upon to pay the interest on those bonds for seven years without recourse, but that there should be included in the amount of the bonds to be guaranteed, a sum sufficient t-o pay interest thereon for three years after completion of the road. The reason put forward by the company in that regard was thai when the road was completed and in operation it would be at least three years before they could gather up traffic-to use the expression which was put forward to us-and put the road in thoroughly good running order for the purposes of securing and carrying traffic.
We thought under the circumstances that the arrangement was a reasonable one. The

faith of the country has been pledged to the enterprise, and it ought to be carried through. While we felt that the Government, so far as the legal aspect of the question is concerned, had a good case, we nevertheless could not fail to be impressed by the fact that the contention of the company was supported by the opinion of very eminent counsel. It seemed therefore that under the circumstances it was a matter for compromise rather than for litigation, inasmuch as litigation would postpone for a very long period the completion of the enterprise, must add materially to the cost, and would render useless and unproductive for a period of perhaps two years $300,000,000 or $350,000,000 already invested in the enterprise by the company and the Government. As the company expressed it to us, the capital invested in the road would remain dead and useless until this additional amount was provided and the road completed to the coast. That, of course, is not absolutely true of the prairie section because that is in operation now. 'But the company have put forward the contention that, until the line is constructed in the prairie provinces, and connected on the one hand with the Pacific, and, on the other hand with Ontario, Quebec and Maritime provinces, and with the lines of the Grand Trunk in. the East, it cannot be expected that these roads in western Canada can be operated with anything like the profit which they eventually will earn when the line is completed from Moncton to Prince Rupert.
The explanation which I have given sets forth in a brief way, and I hope in a clear way, the reasons which have induced the Government to place the proposals before the House. I shall be prepared to go into the matter more fully on the second reading and, this evening, I hope to lay upon the table of the House some documents which relate to the subject and which perhaps will explain more clearly to hon. members the contentroiv on one side or other with regard to the matter which has just been' under negotiation.

The claim of
the Grand Trunk Railway Company for further assistance, as based upon the contracts of 1903 and 1904, does not seem to me to have any legal basis. But the fact remains that the anticipations as to the cost of the road which were entertained in 1903 and 1904 have not been realized and that the construction has cost much more

than, could have 'been expected at that time. The Grand Trunk Pacific may well be supposed to have constructed the line with the greatest economy possible but they had to pay more than was expected at that time for labour and material. Therefore, whilst their claim could not be entertained as a legal claim, and I think the Government was right in that respect, on the other hand, as stated by my right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) the enterprise has to be carried out. At the present time I shall say no more than that we will expect to have this evening all the information possible upon this matter in regard to the application of the Grand Trunk Pacific and more especially as to whether it is expected that the money which is to be expended will be sufficient to complete the road.

I would like to ask my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) whether or not, now that the Government is about granting whatever all hope to be the last measure of assistance for the Grand Trunk Pacific, an arranger ment has been made to close up all matters which are outstanding between the Government and the company and which might operate in any way to prevent the Grand Trunk Pacific from immediately taking-hold of the sections which are now completed and those which may be completed in the near future, and finally taking over the whole line from Prince Bupert to Moncton. A good many rumours have had widespread circulation in tlie newspapers that the Grand Trunk Pacific had made certain objections in respect to the construction of the eastern division. We do know what has [DOT] been stated in the House, that changes have been made in the plans and specifications since this Government came into office, that in many cases velocity grades have been provided for by the commission, that wooden trestles have been erected where the specifications provided for steel, that in some cases wooden bridges have been erected where steel should have been, and that all these changes which have made the road inferior have been made without the consent of the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, as the contract provides. It has been stated in the newspapers-I do not know whether by authority of the Grand Trunk Pacific or not-that in consequence of these changes the Grand Trunk Pacific will not feel bound to enter into a lease for the operation of the eastern
section of the Toad. I speak from the standpoint of the Maritime provinces especially, and I desire to say that in my judgment, unless the Grand Trunk Pacific is to operate the whole line right through to the city of Moncton and thence, either by building independent lines or by using the Intercolonial, to the ports of St. John, Halifax and other eastern cities in the Maritime provinces, the whole national object of this great undertaking will be defeated. We know very well that the Grand Trunk Pacific were desirous in 1903 of only building to North Bay. They had in their mind that when they got to !North Bay they could utilize the Grand Trunk system through Ontario down to Montreal in the summer season, and in the winter they might carry their traffic to Portland in the State of Maine, which has been for many years the winter terminus of the Grand Trunk railway. The late Government was determined that this should not be allowed, and that the road should be carried right through to the port of Quebec, across the St. Lawrence and down to Moncton, so that in bpth summer and winter, as far as possible, this great transcontinental railway should be used for the carriage of traffic through Canadian channels. If the Grand Trunk Pacific has any legal excuse it may decline to enter into a lease for the operation of that portion of the road which is east of Cochrane, and in that event the national object of the undertaking would be defeated.
It does seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that before the Government now enters into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific for a guarantee of $16,000,000, all these outstanding questions ought to be settled. I know that the matter came up when the late Government was in power; there were some outstanding questions and they were brought up and were under consideration just shortly before the election took place in 1911. This is the time for the Government to ascertain what are the questions outstanding, if any; what the objections are, if any, to the Grand Trunk Pacific entering into a lease of those sections which are already completed and having it clearly and distinctly understood that as these sections are completed the Grand Trunk Pacific will take hold of them and operate them and they will enter into a lease, as provided for by the agreement of 1903, to operate the whole line from the Pacific to the Atlantic. I think the Government ought to be able to assure this House, before asking its assent to the Bill, that all

these outstanding questions are settled and that the Grand Trunk Pacific have assured the Government that they will raise no question whatever in regard to entering into a lease. I am particularly impressed with the desirability of bringing the matter before the committee because I find an extraordinary state of affairs existing in regard to the completed section in the province of New Brunswick. This Government has been in office for nearly three years and before the late Government went out of office the Grand Trunk Pacific expressed its willingness to enter into a lease for the operation of the completed section in New Brunswick upon the most reasonable terms which could be imagined. They agreed to operate the road with the necessary train service, with trains running not merely to Moncton, but, if running rights were arranged, to St. John, Halifax and other points in the Maritime provinces served by the Intercolonial railway. They were to operate in this wav, namely, that an account should be kept subject to the supervision of the Government's auditors of the receipts and operating expenses and that, if there should be any deficiency, it should be added to the cost of the Transcontinental road and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should pay interest upon that as well as upon the cost of the road. Nearly three years have passed since this Government have come into office, and no arrangements have been made for the operation of the completed section in New Brunswick, although I believe, it has been completed for nearly two years, because it was operated last year to a certain extent by the commission. My hon.friend the acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) was not able to tell us, when his Estimates were under consideration, whether or not any effort had been made to have an agreement entered into, notwithstandinv the pledge made to this House last session that the mattter would be taken up at once and an effort made to induce the management of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to enter into an agreement. The people of the Maritime provinces are in the dark as to whether or not the management of the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to operate the eastern section of the Transcontinental line. When the Grand Trunk Pacific are coming to Parliament for a grant of $16,000,000, this important question should no longer be left open; the matter should be settled definitely, so that the people will 
know that these valid objections, as to the degrading of the line under the present Government, have been removed; and it would be a matter of gratification to the country, especially to the people of Quebec and the Maritime provinces, to know that this had been done and that an agreement had been entered into.
What objections have the Grand Trunk Pacific made to operating the eastern end of the Transcontinental railway?
In the province of New Brunswick?
Yes, or any part.
That is a matter concerning which the Government ought to tell us.

You are speaking of
objections. Surely you know what the objections are, or do you know that there are any objections?

Yes, I have seen it
stated in the newspapers with authority that the explanation has been made by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company that, by reason of these changes which have been made, they would not be bound to operate the eastern division. I know that, as a matter of law, by reason of the changes in the specification without the consent of the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, they would be able to raise an objection. But now that we are asked to give this large amount of aid, this matter should be made clear. I know that, when asked with regard to the terminals at St. John, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company intimated to the people of St. John that they did not know how they were going to get into St. John, and they really conveyed the impression that they were not entirely certain as to what was going to take place as to the operation of the road in the Maritime provinces. While they did not say that in so many words, that is the impression they conveyed. There is also the important fact that, while about four years ago the Grand Trunk Pacific spent a large amount of money in purchasing some forty or fifty 5 p.m. acres of land at the head of Courtenay Bay at St. John with a view to going ahead with their terminal arrangements immediately, and although Mr. Hays, the late president, had plans prepared showing an extensive layout of the terminals and had stated to the people of

St. John nearly four years ago that the Grand Trunk Pacific wanted to go right ahead so as to have the port ready for the traffic which should come over the Transcontinental railway. During the three years that this Government have been in office, there has not been one advance of any kind or description towards the carrying out of what Mr. Hays then said it was the intention of the company to carry out. I cannot help feeling that, by reason of the changes made without the consent of the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, an uncertainty has been thrown into the minds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as to the intention of the Government with regard to the operation of the eastern division and as to what may be the decision of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Surely it is not unreasonable, now that this question of aid comes up, that these questions should be settled, and that the people should be assured that the Grand Trunk Pacific will not only at once enter upon the operation of the completed sections, but operate the whole line when completed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As to the operation of portions of the line before completion of the whole, I do not understand that the Government have power under the agreement to force the company to operate. The company have the right to elect to operate and the conditions upon which they shall operate are to be settled by agreement or otherwise by arbitration, if I remember correctly.
It is in the statutes of 1904.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, the provision reads:
Pending: the completion of the eastern division by the Government, the company shall be entitled to lease from the commissioners, to be appointed under the said Act, and to operate such portions of the said eastern division as may from time to time be completed, but upon such terms as may be agreed upon between the company and the said commissioners, which terms are not to be more onerous than those of the lease of the whole division by the said contract provided for, save in so far as may be necessary to give full effect to the paramount right of the said commissioners next hereinafter mentioned, and subject always to the paramount right of the said commissioners to use and operate the same without any payment of tolls or other compensation for such purposes as they may deem necessary or expedient in the execution of their commission.
Inasmuch as the arrangement which has been arrived at is not a compromise of a disputed legal right, we did not think it 305
desirable to go into some of the matters to which my hon. friend has alluded, except by way of very general discussion; and I may say that, in so far as that discussion has taken place, we have found no disposition of the part of the company to ask any release of their agreement to operate the eastern division. The only thing that has been discussed, and that more or less in a general way, is as to the date when the operation should begin. Some question was raised as to whether it would be wiser, if the entire road were completed just at the commencement of the winter, to begin the operation in the winter or to await the opening of spring, inasmuch as the road runs through a new country and for a very considerable distance through an uninhabited portion of the country. Doubtless there will be matters to be arranged between the Government and the company in respect of the operation of the eastern division; and the agreement of 1903, as amended by that of 1904, contains quite clear and distinct provisions as to what the respective rights of the Government and the company are to be and as to the manner in which any disputes between the Government and the company are to be disposed of. I do not know whether there is any further agreement we could make that would render it clearer than it is at present The company have put forward, to my knowledge, no claim in respect of the alleged degrading of the road to which my hon. friend alludes.
And I have had conversations- on the whole subject with Mr. Smithers and Mr. Chamberlin. They have insisted very strongly- I am alluding to personal conversations of a recent date-
Did they enter a formal protest?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was speaking of what had taken place during personal negotiations. I think I do remember some allusion to a formal protest. But they have put forward very cogently and insistently that then position has been altered very seriously by reason of the fact that though the prairie section as constructed by them has been opened for operation, (if not formally taken over or formally completed), for about four years and a half, during that time they have had no connection .with the East; and they have urged the claim that if greater expedition had been used in the construction of the line between Winnipeg and Cochrane, they would have been



able to have their connection between the lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the West and the lines of the Grand Trunk in the East. And they attach to that failure what seems to be an exaggerated importance. They have put it forward as meaning a very great loss to them. I have not admitted any claim in that regard, nor any claim 'whatever. That has been the subject of the most frequent discussions in the negotiations that have been carried on in regard to this matter. I have had no intimation whatever from the company, either directly or indirectly, that they are not prepared to carry out the terms of the agreement entered into by the company in 1903 as amended by the agreement of 1904.

On section 1:
Will my hon. friend explain the motive of the Bill.
