speechtext:
I will. My right hon.
friend remembers that by section 9 of chapter 71 of the Statutes of 1903 it was provided that the construction of the eastern division of the National Transcontinental railway should be carried on by three commissioners. I think the number of commissioners may afterwards have been increased.
Four.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In 1912, it was provided by chapter 39 of the statutes of that year that one commissioner might be appointed, and during the last two and a half years Major R. W. Leonard has been commissioner under the legislation as so amended. It is hoped that the road will be completed during the present year. The contracts have long since been let, and everything else of importance in that regard has been done. It is possible that the private business affairs of Major Leonard may not permit

him in the future to discharge the 'duties of commissioner. It is thought that within the few months or weeks that might elapse, it would be the proper thing so to amend the section that the Minister of Railways himself might exercise the powers and discharge the duties of the commissioner. That explains the first subsection.
As to the second subsection: The commissioners have power, under the agreement of 1904, amending in that respect the scheduled agreement of 1903, to operate the eastern division before completion. Perhaps I had better read the enactments. By section 9 of chapter 71 of the Statutes of 1903,
' it was provided as follows:
The construction of the eastern division and the operation thereof until completed and leased to the company pursuant to the provisions of the agreement shall be under the charge and control of three commissioners, to be appointed by the Governor in Council, who shall hold office during pleasure, and who, and whose successors in office, shall be a body corporate under the name of ' the Commissioners of the Transcontinental Railway ' and are hereinafter called ' the Commissioners.'
By section 3 of the Schedule to the National Transcontinental Railway Act, chapter 24 of the Statutes of 1904, it was provided:
3. Pending the completion of the eastern division by the Government, the company shall be entitled to lease from the commissioners, to be appointed under the said Act, and to operate such portions of the said eastern division as may from time to time be completed, but upon such terms as may be agreed upon between the company and the said commissioners, which terms are not to be more onerous than those of the lease of the whole division by the said contract provided for, save in so far as may be necessary to give full effect to the paramount right of the said commissioners next hereinafter mentioned, and subject always to the paramount right of the said commissioners to use and operate the same without any payment of tolls or other compensation for such purposes as they may deem necessary or expedient in the execution of their commission.
In view of the fact that it is proposed that the minister may be appointed to exercise the powers and discharge the duties of commissioner, and that a certain period might intervene between the completion of the road and the time when the company should undertake the operation thereof under lease, it is thought desirable that the minister should be vested with power to operate the whole or any part of the eastern division as a Government railway, in order to ensure that the road shall be operated immediately after completion, and to render it practically impossible that any considerable period should

intervene between the technical completion of the road and the leasing of it to the company.
At what time is it expected that the section of the road between Winnipeg and Quebec will be completed and taken over by the company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
During the coming
autumn, but as I stated a moment ago in speaking upon the other Bill, some question has been raised by the company as to whether or not, if the whole line should be completed this autumn it would be desirable to begin operation during the winter months, or whether it would be more in the interests of the country and of the company as well to begin operations early in the spring. That matter, however, has not been decided in any way.
Assuming that the road is completed this fall, will the section west of Cochrane be put in operation whether the section from Cochrane to Quebec is ready for operation or not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Government, as I
understand the contract, has no power to compel the company to take a lease of a portion of the line. The company has the right to ask that it may operate a portion of the line and that an agreement be made for that purpose. It does not seem to me that we could force the company to operate that portion of the line alone, but the passing of this enactment will give to the Minister of Railways and Canals power to operate it himself if he should think fit to do so.

The object of this Bill, as explained by my hon. friend, is to vest in the Minister of Railways the powers now vested in the commissioner. As to the motive, my hon. friend says that the road is on the point of being completed and that there will, therefore, be no further need for the services of the commissioner.
I should be glad indeed to believe that the expectations of my hon. friend with regard to the completion of the road will be realized. There is no doubt whatever that the roadbed will be completed this season; in fact it was to have been completed ere this. But the road will not be finished simply because the roadbed is ready; terminals and various other accommodations will	be necessary. My hon.
friend is	aware that	there are
no terminals at all at Quebec and that if, as expected, the roadbed is completed in 3051
November, there will be no stations or terminals. I understand that the contract has been let for a freight station to be erected on the old Champlain market site. As to the passenger station itself, an agreement was entered into by Major Leonard, sanctioned by the Government, under which a union station was to be built for the Canadian Pacific railway and the National Transcontinental-railway. It was supposed that this agreement, which was made last year, would be followed by definite action, but up to the present time nothing has been done in the way of carrying it out. I do not know even if the land has been purchased, but I am certain that the plans respecting this station have not been carried out. The workshops have been established at St. Malo. It was first decided to have them located at Cap Rouge, but it was finally decided to place them some eight miles from the roadway, at a place which is not accessible by rail. How access will be obtained to that place from the roadway is a matter which has not yet been settled. It was rumoured at one time that a tunnel was to be built from the roadway to the workshops, but nothing has been done. I have reason to believe that at the present time the Government have not made any arrangements to establish communication with the workshops at St. Malo. The other day the acting Minister of Railways told me that access would be obtained by arrangement with the Canadian Northern or with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The shops are placed in proximity to the lines of the Canadian Pacific and Canadian Northern railways, but they are eight miles from the railway which they are intended to serve. To obtain access to these workshops, one of three things must be done. We must have a line from our own railway to the workshops; we must make an arrangement with the Canadian Northern railway or we must make an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific railway. Nothing has been done, however, along that line. Unfortunately, the road is far from being completed. I do not think that it can be completed this season, and even if a load of grain were to come over the railway from Winnipeg to Quebec, there would be no station to receive it. The situation, therefore, is not at all J3 represented by my hon. friend. As the road is far from being completed, there is no immediate necessity for doing away with the services of the commissioner and vesting his powers in the Minister of Railways. If the road were to be com-

pleted within a few months, perhaps there would be no objection to the Minister of Railways taking charge of the National Transcontinental railway. In 1904, when this legislation was introduced, we thought it proper to place the construction of the road under the control of a commission. When my hon. friend came into power in 1911, he did not abandon the idea of a commission, but he modified it and placed the railway in the hands of a single commissioner, Major Leonard. I am not sure that Miajor Leonard has made a great success of it so far; at all events I think it is altogether hopeless to assume that the road will be completed during the present year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The station at the Champlain market is not a freight station alone; it is a passenger and freight station combined.
It is stated in the press that the building which is now being erected on the Champlain market site is simply a freight shed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is a mistake; it is a passenger and freight station, costing about 870,000 and, as I am informed, it has been approved by the authorities of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. The plans have been submitted to them and they have approved of them. Two agreements have been worked out respecting the union station, and the city of Quebec was a party, I think to at least one of them. One agreement was for the construction of the station and the other for its management and operation. A great deal of negotiation went on in respect of both of those agreements but they, were finally completed, 1 think several weeks or perhaps months ago. After they were completed some question arose, I am not familiar with the exact details, as to the acquisition of land. The Canadian Pacific railway proposed to put in certain lands and I think the Government were going to acquire and put in certain lands also, and it appears that some difficulties, the exact nature of which I do not recall at the moment, arose which caused- some further delay. I understand the difficulties have now all been removed and I am informed that the Canadian Pacific railway was to call for tenders for the construction of the station at a very early date. I am not prepared to say just what length of time will be required for its construction, but in the meantime, the station at t'he Champlain [Sir Wilfrid Laurier.J
market will be available and will answer temporary needs.
As far as the tunnel is concerned, there has been more than one proposal submitted to the commissioners by their engineers and considered by them. I am not prepared to say at the moment whether a final conclusion has been reached as to which scheme is to be adopted. My right hon. friend has referred to a piece of line which I think is vested in the Canadian Northern railway and which would provide access to the union station when constructed. That line of railway would also provide access to the shops. I understand that arrangements are practically completed for the acquisition by the Government of that line of the Canadian Northern railway. I do not wish to give that as an assurance, but I understand from the acting Minister of Railways that arrangements were practically fcomplefted to-day for its asquisition which would provide, pending the construction of the tunnel, access to the union station and to the shops at St. Malo. Under the circumstances, I could hardly agree with my right hon. friend as to the difficulty in respect of terminals in the meantime. It will be found that these terminals will be ready by the time the roadbed and the necessary accessories are completed in such a way as to permit the operation of the road. We feel very sure that our expectations in that regard will not be disappointed.

If there was any definiteness about the date of the completion of this line, there would be some reason for this Bill; but this line is not completed and unless the Government are going to declare in an arbitrary way that it is completed before it really is, its completion is many months away. Major Leonard remains commissioner until the road is completed? The Bill does not seem to outline that. I think it is an open secret that there has been lack of harmony between Major Leonard and some members of the Government for quite a long time. If we may judge by some articles which appear in the Winnipeg Telegram and in a certain newspaper in Quebec to which the Postmaster General is very close, these papers have been condemning Major Leonard for months. It is said that this trouble arose because Major Leonard has a very stiff backbone and refuses to allow the commission to be run on political lines; that he has maintained his position under the statute to manage the affairs of the Grand Trunk Pacific, as far as construction is concerned, and that

he has done as his judgment dictated, that he was being really interfered with at every turn, and consequently, whoever was right or whoever was wrong, friction arose. I am inclined to think that this Bill might have a short title, ' A Bill to dispense with the services of Major Leonard.' Without any frills as to the details, I really think that is what it is for, from information that X have had coming to me for the last three or four months. I think that the public will agree that a mess has been made of the situation in the city of Quebec. Everything has been left at a standstill, in fact it has been turned backwards in that city during the past two and a half years. When this Government came into power they found a pretty well defined plan, first a station at the Champlain market, with a line nearly constructed to that station from the Transcontinental. That site for the station was chosen by consent of the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Quebec Central, the Delaware and Hudson, the city council of Quebec, the Board of Trade of Quebec and the Government. Several meetings were held and a unanimous arrangement was agreed upon by all the parties. The Champlain market and other property was purchased for the completion of this work. The shops were to be placed where the shops ought to be, on the main line of the Transcontinental near the north end of the Quebec bridge; and there is no railway man, unless he is interested, who will give any other decision. I am doubtful if the chief engineer of the Transcontinental railway has given his consent to all that has been going on in the city of Quebec with regard to the Transcontinental. If he has not, then that work is in direct contravention of the statute. He is the responsible man, more responsible in a way than the chief commissioner himself; and I cannot bring myself to think that Gordon Grant has agreed to what has been done in Quebec and around it with the National Transcontinental railway. The shops were to be constructed approximately at the north end of the Quebec bridge on the main line of the Transcontinental, and any repairs that had to be made on ears for through traffic going to the Maritime provinces, or from them, could be dropped within a stone's throw of the main line and there repaired and put in service again. These shops have been changed and taken seven or eight miles away from the main line of the Transcontinental, and if you do buy the Canadian Northern railway you
are at that much more expense, although this Government were going to be more economical than we were. In addition to that, every car and engine has to be hauled seven miles and back again over that line, a haulage of fourteen miles to the shops; and these shops are for the benefit of two other roads and not for that of the Transcontinental railway. I say it advisedly, and I have discussed the subject a good deal, that a mess, and a horrible mess, has been made of the Transcontinental at Quebec. While it may be that the road will have the steel laid and will be ballasted and all that kind of thing this autumn, the provision at Quebec will not be completed and cannot Ibe for taking care of the traffic, and we will find that if traffic can be brought to Quebec that there will be no facilities there to take care of it. Every person will agree, the Postmaster General cannot but agree with me in what his newspaper has said, that the work has been retarded beyond all the endurance and patience of the people of Quebec during the last year. Who was to blame I do not know, but I do believe that friction has occurred between the commissioner and the Government, and that that is responsible to a great extent for the condition in Quebec at the present time. If the commissioner is to remain until the road is completed, he ought to remain at least one year more, and even then Quebec will not be ready for the traffic. If ever there is a time when a commissioner is needed it is at the completion of the road. Just when it has to be decided whether a particular portion of the line has been constructed according to contract, and whether the agreement between the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Transcontinental and the Government has been carried out in all its details, and whether the terminals have been properly constructed-that is the time when a strong commissioner is needed, and it. is the worst time of all to take the road out of the hands of the commissioner and put it in the hands of the Government unless for very good reasons. If this Bill is to get rid of Major Leonard the Government ought to take Parliament into its confidence and say so. If they are not satisfied with the way Major Leonard has conducted the business of the construction of this road and consequently they propose to take over the management of the road themselves, they ought to say so. The Government did not like the commis-

sion they found when they came into power, and dispensed with its services. They said there was going to be a great improvement; they were going to appoint as a one-man commission a man of high repute. I am not going to criticise Major Leonard at all, but I say emphaticaly that nobody knows better than the Government that they have been in constant trouble ever since the commission was changed, either through their owm fault or the fault of the commissioner or some of the officials. If it is proposed to remove Major Leonard on account of the breach between him and the Government, a6 I believe, I urge the Government to tell us that that is the case. If the Government would have this House believe that this step is merely in anticipation of the road being completed, then I say they are all wTong because the road will not be completed this year not yet next year unless they make better progress than has been made in the past two years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend seems to misunderstand the terms of the Bill as well as its purpose. The Bill does not provide that the Minister of Railways and Canals shall be the commissioner. It merely provides that he shall be eligible to be appointed as commissioner. If it should prove that Major Leonard is unable to continue in the discharge of his duties by reason of his own personal affairs, the Government would be face to face with one of two alternatives: either to appoint a commissioner in succession to him, or to have the Minister of Railways and Canals take over the work. My hon. friend will realize that to get a suitable man who would undertake to discharge the duties of commissioner for possibly only six months or a year would be practically impossible, and mere-fore it has been thought desirable that this Act should be amended in this way. The Bill is not designed for the purpose of getting rid of Major Leonard, as my hon. friend suggests. Personally, I have had very little to do with Major Leonard; the most I have had to do with him was in connection with the Quebec terminals, to which my hon. friends have alluded. Before speaking in Quebec last autumn, I asked him to come and explain to me the whole situation in regard to the terminal at Quebec. I asked him to give me a full and frank description of the position, and to state to me definitely whether or not the terminals would be ready and sufficient to take care of the traffic by the time the road

was completed. He gave me a statement, and after having first submitted that statement to him in writing to see whether it was in consonance with his arrangements and intentions, I embodied it in the statement I made to the people of Quebec. I see no reason to believe that he will not be able to carry out what he then told me he was prepared to carry out. For the reason that I intended to make an important statement to the people of Quebec, I desired above everything else to be absolutely accurate. As I have already said, I called in Major Leonard, and listened with the greatest care and attention to his description of the proposed work in connection with the terminals at Quebec. I took notes, and afterwards dictated a statement to my stenographer. I revised that statement after it had been dictated, and submitted it to Major Leonard for his perusal before I delivered it in the city of Quebec. Therefore, so far as that statement	is concerned, which	was regarded as satisfactory by the people of Quebc, to whom it was communicated, I say that I have the warrant of Major Leonard for every word that I uttered on that occasion. I can say further that so far as my communication with him in respect to that matter is concerned, I found him most ready to inform me, and he has been of the greatest possible assistance so far as my personal relations with him are concerned. I have never had the slightest cause to complain of any incident or anything whatever in respect of his discharge of his duties as commissioner.
I would like to say also that the changes which were made in the arrangements planned by the former commission have not been brought about through any political influence whatever, so far as I understand and so far as I believe. The changes which were made were advised by Major Leonard, so the Minister of Railways and Canals informs me. They were urged upon the Minister of Railways and Canals as changes for the better, and (inasmuch as we had appointed Major Leonard as commissioner, and as the terms of the statute vested a very .large discretion in him, it would hardly have been becoming for the Government to set up its will against the will of the commissioner who had been selected for his great experience in matters of this kind. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) states his belief

that Mr. Grant, the chief engineer of the Transcontinental, has not acquiesced in these changes. I am not able of my own personal knowledge to state whether that is or is not the case, but I shall make inquiry. I can only say at the moment that I shall be very much surprised to learn that the changes have not been acquiesced in and approved of by Mr. Grant. At the moment I cannot say more than that, because I desire to be accurate in any representation or statement that I make before the committee in respect of so important a matter. I have always understood that Mr. Grant did acquiesce, and I certainly know that these changes were urged by Major Leonard.

I was not criticising
Major Leonard, I was rather saying that he had been pushed pretty strongly on other grounds than that of railway practice, and that friction had frequently arisen. I have a very high opinion of Major Leonard in a good many ways, although I differ from him in some of his contentions as to the railway. It has been rumoured that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, which is to lease these terminals at Quebec-and when I say terminals I refer to everything included in the changes at Quebec-ha3 not given its formal consent to all these changes although they cannot properly be carried out without the consent of that company. Is that true?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I desire to speak with
reserve on that matter as I do not profess to be fully informed of the facts.
I will make inquiry and give the information at a later date. I understand that, although the approval of the Grand Trunk Pacific may not have been given in formal, legal shape, all these proposals from time to time and the plans which accompanied them have been submitted to them, and they have acquiesced in and approved of them in an informal way. That is my understanding at the moment. I shall make inquiry and obtain definite information before this Bill shall have passed its third reading.

The question was raised in another discussion as to the company contending that the line would not be completed until the Quebec bridge was finished. I think the acting Minister of Railways and Canals will find a letter from the late Mr. Hays admitting that the completion of the bridge was not a necessary part of the
completion of the Transcontinental railway. That is on file somewhere.
There will be no difficulty about that.

Speaking also with great reserve, I would say that I have reason to believe that up to the present time the Grand Trunk Pacific have not assented to the changes which have been made in the Quebec terminals. It may be true that they have been communicated with from time to time as to the nature of these changes, but my information is that the Grand Trunk Pacific have never assented to these changes, but on the contrary have protested against them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend refer to any particular part of the work or generally?

No, generally to the character of the road and the changes in the Quebec station and terminals. If I understood my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways and Canals and the Prime Minister the Government have acquired the line of the Canadian Northern railway from St. Malo to Cap Rouge.

There is a short piece of line five miles long, extending from the viaduct to the St. Malo shops. Negotiations have been going on for some time with the owners of the railway for the purpose of acquiring it, and the negotiations, I understand, were concluded to-day.
How could you acquire that line without any authority?
We have made an offer which has been accepted.
That simply means more delay?
In what way?

To-day the hon. gentleman says the negotiations are completed. Where is your authority for acquiring that line of railway? I do not know that you have any. I do not know under what statute you can acquire that road. Has the agreement been signed?
No, the agreement has not been signed. The negotiations were only completed to-day for the purpose of acquiring the road.

That means more delay. I understand the Government are building a station at Champlain

market to cost $70,000. I speak subject to correction, because it is some time since I have seen the contract, but I am under the impression that the contract which was made with the city of Quebec for the erection of a station at Champlain market had as one of its conditions that the station to be built was to cost $1,000,000, and that is the reason why the land was sold for $100,000. I do not make an absolute statement to that effect, because I may be wrong, but I am sure that the station that we intended to build when we gave the eontract in 1911 was to cost $1,000,000. Would my hon. friend be kind enough to place a plan of the station before the House?
Yes. I personally submitted a plan of the station at Champlain market to Mr. Chamberlin, and he approved of the plan upon which tenders are being called.
My hon. friend will put a plan of the station and also the approval of Mr. 'Chamberlin on the table?

I showed it to Mr. Chamberlin and he agreed.
- Sir WILFRID LAURIER: Oh, my hon. friend is satisfied with that?

I think it would be wise now to have the formal approval of rue Grand Trunk Pacific to the changes in Quebec. As to the acquisition of this portion of the Canadian Northern line, the Prime Minister will agree with me in saying that there is no authority under the Act for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific to buy a piece of line. Everything has to be advertised for and tenders asked. We had a great deal of correspondence and difficulty in working out the details in order to take over the contract that the old Quebec Bridge Company had for the construction of the connection between Champlain market and the Quebec bridge. The line was partly constructed and it took several weeks to work out a way to take over that contract. The price was lower than that which we had received for similar work elsewhere. I do not think there is any power at all to take over that line and if the line is to be taken over a vote will have to be placed in the Supplementary Estimates during the present session in order to authorize it, or another agreement will have to be confirmed, or some other steps taken by Parliament authorizing you to take over the line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would not be prepared to express an opinion one way or the other without making an examination of the statute. It may be possible that legislation will be required for the purpose. The hon. gentleman will remember that, with respect to about six miles west of Winnipeg, legislation was necessary for the purpose of making it a part of the western division of the National Transcontinental railway. The road was owned by some other company; I do not remember which company it was.

I think the Canadian
Northern.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is my impression.
In the same way it may be that legislation will have to be enacted in regard to this. But I will know more about it perhaps when we come to deal with it later.

It should be done with
the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific because they will have to pay interest upon that line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will have all this information when we come again to deal with the matter.
As a matter of fact, has the Government turned down any of Major Leonard's actions in respect of the Quebec works?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know exactly
what my hon. friend means by ' turning down.'
Is there a conflict between the Government and Major Leonard as regards the Quebec work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The only thing I recall
at the moment is that I think Major Leonard was under the impression that a smaller and less expensive station than that which is to be erected would be sufficient for the requirements at Champlain market but it was thought that a station such as is proposed would be more suitable, and he acquiesced in that upon the reasons being put forward.
Is he going to leave the service of the Government completely?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not said that he was going to leave before the completion of the road, but I spoke of the possibility of his private affairs requiring his attention, and in that way I mentioned that during the short time which would intervene the

Minister of Railways might be trusted to perforin the duties of the commissioner.

That is very satisfactory, but for my right hon. friend's information, because there must be only one mind as regards the situation between the authorities and the people in Quebec, I desire to read to my right hon. friend something which I find here in a Conservative paper, the Quebec Chronicle:
I have here the organ of the Conservative party, the Quebec Chronicle, an editorial in which, under date of Quebec, June 3, 1914, reads as follows:
Transcontinental Commission.	.
The end of Major Leonard as National Transcontinental railway commissioner is in sight. It is known that for some time he has disagreed with some of the most influential members of the Cabinet and that some of the most important Quebec works have been delayed, because he insisted too much on having eveiything his own way. At all events, the Government is now introducing a Bill allowing them to transfer the work of the Transcontinental Comnvs-sion to the Minister of Railways and Canals.
In the firm hand of the Hon. Mr. Cochrane, who will now direct and decide in place of Major Leonard, it is expected that the work of the terminals will be proceeded with much more satisfactorily than before. It is known that Major Leonard had at last consented to invite tenders on the first plan for the Champlain market station, leaving to one side the plans, or the small bit of a station which he had prepared. Tenders were due yesterday and it is likely that the contract will be let without any unnecessary delay.
This station, such as it will be built, will, we understand, be an ornament to the river front and is arranged in such a way that any number of freight sheds may be added on the western side.
Just here in parenthesis-my hon. friend will remember, during the first session of this Parliament, after the address had been adopted by 'this House, my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition moved for the papers in connection with this station. Up jumped the Postmaster General and said:	Nine-tenths of the people
in Quebec know that the Champlain market station is a blunder, and that it should never have been located there. Here now, we have the announcement that this station on the Champlain market will be an ornament to the river front and will be arranged in such a way that any number of freight sheds may be added on the western side. Just the argument made by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition.
Mr. Cochrane has submitted a final Order in Council for the Quebec union passenger and
freight station at the Palais and the Canadian Pacific railway has been notified that everything is in readiness in that respect.
Of course, no mention of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company is satisfied.
There also seems to be no doubt that Major Leonard's brand new scheme of a tunnel under the Laval University-
Which is the heart of Quebec.
That is not the place.

(reading):
-with level crossings on St. Paul and St. Andrew streets, main business thoroughfares of Quebec, will be discarded and that some of the St. Malo shops which Major Leonard omitted from the plans will now be proceeded with.
That has reference to the plans made by the land speculators.
Major Leonard had also strongly objected-
He is an oppositionist.
-that there should be so much accommodation	contemplated on the rivef
front, and he thought that what the Harbour Board was doing in the estuary of the St. George river was sufficient. On this point also Major Leonard's view will not prevail any more and the Government have put in the Supplementary Estimates the sum of $500,000 to begin work on the river front, under the direction of the Minister of Public Works.
It is gratifying to learn that these works which have been held hack will now he carried out witti fresh impetus.
The elections are coming next year.
That it should he so is almost wholly due to the good work of Hon. L. P. Pelletier.

It is a good newspaper. I have reason to believe that what the Chronicle says is to a great extent the view not only of its editor but of the Quebec Board of Trade, the mayor of Quebec and the city council of Quebec.

Is it the view of the
Government?
The Government expresses its views on the floor of the House.
Not always.
An honest Government like this one always does. There is no use disguising the fact that there are complaints in Quebec because the work has not been proceeded with. There is no denying that fact.
About whom are the people in Quebec complaining?

They are complaining about Major Leonard in that respect.

There is correspondence between the Board of Trade and Major Leonard and between the mayor of Quebec and Major Leonard.

Who appointed Major
Leonard?
Does my hon. friend not know that yet; I thought he knew more than that.

The Government gave
and the Government are taking away.
Blessed be the name of the Government.

The union station at
Quebec, the Champlain Market station, the workshops-the tout ensemble as now outlined, has been suggested by Major Leonard. It has been approved by the Minister of Railways and it has met with the approval of the citizens of Quebec. There is not the slightest doubt about that, because the city council has passed a resolution, practically unanimously, agreeing to all these changes. There is no use for my hon. friend to pretend that this is objected to by the people of Quebec, because it is not. There is dissatisfaction on account of the delay, mainly on account of the Champlain Market station.
I myself am of the opinion that it might have been begun before.
You were opposed to it.
That is a scheme of which I entirely approve.
The Champlain station?
The little one?

No, I was against the little one. I am in favour of the big one.
I am in favour of the one which this Government is building. Is not that satisfactory to my hon. friends on the other side?
When did you change your mind?

I never changed my mind on this question. The plan which Major Leonard had Was not satisfactory to the people of Quebec, and was opposed by the people and the city council. The moment they got a business scheme and plan, like the one now in course of completion, they accepted it with the greatest pleasure and put themselves on record in that respect.

Would the plan include the tunnel?
	[
What does my hon. friend mean by that?
Just a tunnel to go under the ground. Does the plan, which the people of Quebec said was a business plan and which they approved, include the tunnel?
Yes, it does.
Mr. Cochrane says it should be wiped away.

\ly hon. friend has not listened attentively. There have been two plans, both suggested by the Transcontinental Commission. The first one my hon. friend referred to the other day and said it had been discarded. He said also that the St. Malo shops had been discarded.
No, I never said that.

He said they were
shown on the map as discarded.

I said they had been
marked off the map.

That is practically
the same thing. Another plan, for a tunnel under the city of Quebec has been deposited in the registry office. This was done by the Transcontinental Railway Commission. The people of Quebec are opposed to this last proposition. The City Council is opposed to it, the Board of Trade is opposed .to it. It is not surprising, under these circumstances, that the newspapers in Quebec should voice the public opinion about it. There is the whole matter. I invite my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid. Laurier), and the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) to wait and see, when these plans are completed and this work executed, who will be right and who will be wrong.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. A. LACHANCE (Quebec Centre,). (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to take part in the debate on the Bill now submitted to the consideration of the House, and I would not have changed my mind in the matter, had not the question of the establishment of the Transcontinental terminals in the city of Quebec cropped up incidentally.
Having in the course of the recent debate on the report of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton dealt with various matters

to which reference was made this afternoon, I was anxious to know what answer the government would make to the statements I made at the time. I therefore listened very attentively to the speeches of the right hon. the Prime Minister, of the hon. {Postmaster General and of the hon. Minister of Customs. To my regret, 1 must aver that the only inference that can be drawn from their utterances, is that, as regards these terminals, no advance has been made within the last three years and that the government are still in a state of absolute indecision concerning their future plans in this connection.
Those who were present during the debate may have noticed, as well as myself, the hesitation with which these hon. gentlemen ventured to tread on that ground; vagueness and indefiniteness characterized all their statements. However, the hon. Postmaster General has requested us to wait a while, and that we would have convincing proofs of the efficiency of this government.
All the same, I am not satisfied; for three years wonderful things have been promised to Quebec, but Quebec is still awaiting the fulfilment of any of one of those promises.
When I recall the rabid denunciations of the Quebec Conservative papers, such as the Evenement, the Morning Chronicle, etc., previous to September 21,	1911,
in respect to the so-called inactivity of the then government in the matter of the Transcontinental terminals, I am surprised at the mildness shown by those papers, whose editors, these three years have abstained from calling attention to the inactivity of our ministers, and whenever they uttered a sound, did so with the object of excusing the government and holding responsible for any delay some official in the latter's employ. I am the more surprised that during the last session the hon. Postmaster General seemed intent on assuming the full responsibility of the change effected in the original plans of such terminals, and I am happy to find that his stand at this moment confirms me in that view. He was anxious, no doubt, to impress the whole world in that way with a high opinion of his power and prestige in the councils of the state. But the fame he won in that way must have vanished considerably in the meantime, for events have turned out contrary to his expectations, and that responsibility of which he was so proud, must now weigh on his shoulders like a
leaden cloak. That recalls to my mind some verses of Dante's Divine Comedy, wherein the poet describes the fate of unfortunate men bending under the weight of such a mantle, condemned to unceasingly turn within the same circle, over steep precipices, and forced in the course of their grim pilgrimage to pass over the bodies of victims of the executioner.
The position in which the hon. Postmaster General now is appears Jo /me somewhat similar; there is no opening for him through which to escape, in whatever direction lie turns. How much lighter he would feel, if only he could cast aside that mantle; but that is out of question. Indeed, of late, he has been obliged to ride over the body of his friend, Mr. Leonard, who no doubt was his close advisor in the preparation of the new plans of the Transcontinental terminals; for I do not suppose for a single moment that this gentleman would have touched these plans at. all without the assistance of the hon. minister. However, less merciful than those unfortunate people to whom I have just referred, the hon. minister not only passed over the body of his friend, but I might add that he trampled it under foot. I find evidence of the fact in two editorials published in the Evenement of Quebec, on May 4. and 5, 1914. That paper is the organ of the hon. Postmaster General. They contain strictures of a violent character in reference to that quondam bosom friend. Persons who are familiar with the turn of mind and the manner of writing of the hon. gentlemen state that these denunciations must be attributed to him. I have reason to believe that they are right in stating so. Whether they are right or wrong, I may be allowed to quote those two editorials. In the first place, the article appearing in the Evenement of Monday, May 4, 1914, reads as follows: The Stations and Workshops.
Spring is with us once more, and, as often happens in our clime, hardly has the snow melted away, than without transition summer is heralded in by a succession of warm days. The harbour awakens and gives signs of greater activity. More than fifteen steamers have entered it since the opening of navigation. Work is proceeding on all sides; it seems as though the number of hands were not sufficient to cope with the requirements. This is the proper time to take a hand in the work and to deal earnestly with the question of the great public improvements which are proposed, or in course of execution, at Quebec.
If we are unwilling to fritter away part of the already too short season which is just opening, tenders should be called for immediately for the building of the Champlain market station. As regards the Union station at the Palais,

have done absolutely nothing towards the building of these terminals within the last three years, and they will have to bear the responsibility of that neglect, which may have possibly disastrous results for Quebec as well as for the whole Canada.

I do not rise to make a long speech or to follow in detail the various points raised by the hon. member for Quebec Centre. He has evidenced a great deal of cleverness and wit; he has read articles from the newspapers and commented upon them with a good deal of apparent satisfaction, and I shall do nothing which will in any way detract from his satisfaction in this matter. While the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec Centre may be very witty, they are not at all to the point. He said that last year I took the responsibility of carrying out the plans for the terminals at Quebec. So I did, and I do the same thing to-day. I have always taken the ground that the plan outlined by the former Transcontinental Commission was not what was needed in respect of the terminals at Quebec, and I think so still. The complaint urged by the Board of Trade and the City Council of Quebec is that the work should have been begun early this spring. It was not begun early because the tenders for the Champlain Market station had not been called for as soon as the people of Quebec would have desired. At all events, tenders have been asked and received and I expect that before many days are over the contract will be let. The Government will be in a position to give the contract to the lowest tenderer, and I hope that the lowest tenderer will execute his work promptly and well. I may add, in all fairness and justice to Major Leonard, that he has always declared that this station will be ready at the time of the completion of the road. Whether or not this prediction will be fulfilled time will tell, but, in any case, this work will not be delayed; the contract will be let at once.
The hon. member for Quebec Centre and the right hon. leader of the Opposition have repeated what they have seen in the newspapers with regard to this matter. The Liberal papers of Quebec are full of complaints. They find fault with everything; they say that the new arrangement for the terminals, which received the approval of of the people of Quebec, of the city council and of the board1 of trade, has not been approved by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Le Soleil, the organ of my

aright hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, and the other English-speaking Liberal papers have published that statement time and again. As a matter of fact, the contracts for the building of the union station and for its operation were entered into after the matter was fully discussed in my presence in the office of the Minister of Railways, fully discussed with Mr. Biggar, the general counsel of the Grand Trunk railway, and with Mr. Kelley, one of the vice-presidents of the company. My hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways was there also, in the absence of the Minister of Railways, and these terms were agreed upon in our presence. These are the facts, and they cannot be denied. About ten days ago I asked Mr. Chamberlin how he could account for the fact that the Liberal press in Quebec were making the statement that he did not approve these plans. He said that he never authorized anybody to make such a declaration. His grievance was that when these contracts had been actually signed, after they had been approved by his company and his representative, Major Leonard should have notified him of the fact, and that he did not do so. I shall not give any opinion as to that, it is a mere matter of detail.
As to the other works at Quebec, my hon. friend, no doubt in good faith, has made a big mistake. He tells us that the Champlain Market station is not being built according to the contract between the city of Quebec and the Transcontinental Commission and that the mayor of Quebec made a complaint to that effect at a recent meeting of the city council. I told my hon. friend when he said that that he was entirely mistaken, and I say again that he is entirely mistaken. As a matter of fact, the station on the Champlain market is not mentioned in the contract between the Transcontinental Commission and the city of Quebec, and my hon. friend, who represents one of the important divisions of Quebec, surely ought to know that. Yet he comes before this committee and tells hon. gentlemen that the mayor is complaining that the station is not going to be built according to the contract. Evidently my hon. friend has something more to learn with regard to this matter. The contract between the Transcontinental Commission and the city of Quebec has reference to the St. Malo shops and the union station, and not to the Champlain Market station. I hape that my hon. friend will in future be careful of the facts

in referring to this matter and that he will relate only those circumstances which are within his knowledge. Having devoted a great deal of thought, time and labour to this matter with a view of bringing it to a final issue, I know exactly how it stands, and I repeat that my hon. friend made a huge mistake when he accused this Government and Major Leonard of not fulfilling the contract to which he refers. The shops were begun last fall; the contractors worked nearly all winter, and a great deal of progress has been made on them. The work is progressing now. There are a great many employees working at it today. The construction of the Champlain Market station will begin within a few days. As to the union station, there has been a good deal of difficulty and discussion between the Canadian Pacific railway and the Transcontinental Commission. These difficulties have been adjusted after a great deal of work and after many efforts to have them settled. They are now settled, I am happy to say, and I hope that the work will proceed before long. Those are the facts and I shall not detain tjje committee at any length about them. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) said there had been a big mess made in connection with the Quebec terminals. I might tell him that, if there is some disappointment at Quebec because the other works have not begun as early this spring, as they might have done, the people of Quebec are absolutely united, except, of course, the Liberal papers which have to find fault anyway. The Quebec people, Liberal and Conservative, are a unit in thinking that the plans now completed and the work which is going to be finished are the proper ones and meet the views of every one who has the interest of Quebec at heart. That is what the hon. member for South Renfrew calls a mess.
It is a mess from the standpoint of the Transcontinental; it is not in the interests of that railway.

Not at all, it is in the interests of the Transcontinental and future events will prove that the Transcontinental Railway terminals at Quebec will not be confined, as they would have been under the former Administration, to one large station. While there was some space between the cliff and the river front, that area was not large enough for a station of that importance without blocking everything else. We were all of that opinion. I was of that opinion when plans for the 306
station were adopted, when the tenders were invited; and we were so strongly of that opinion, one and all, that when we came into power we cancelled that contract, and now Quebec is going to have two stations as terminals for the Grand Trunk Pacific, a fine station at the Palais, both freight and passenger, and another smaller station at the Champlain market, freight and passenger also. This is satisfactory to the people of Quebec and they do not complain of it at all. They do complain of certain delay, but after all it is better to have delay and have the work properly done than to rush work which would not be a success in the end.

I have a very strong
objection to the second section. I want to know what it mean3. I would also like to call the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to section 3, because it relates to eastern Canada and to the operation of the line in the Maritime provinces. Section 3 provides:
After the eastern division is completed and until it is leased to- the company the said eastern division shall he under the control and management of the Minister of Railways and Canals, who shall have power to operate the whole or any part of the said division as a Government railway under the provisions of the Government Railways Act, Revised Statutes, 1906, chapter 36.
If my right hon. friend is not in a position to disclaim any intention of providing that the Government may operate a portion of the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific another portion, I would necessarily have a suspicion that this section is intended to provide for the very thing which we in the lower provinces, and also many people in the province of Quebec, are afraid of. We have heard rumours for quite a while, and statements have been made in the newspapers, that * is the intention in quarters which are influential and powerful to induce the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate the line from Winnipeg to Cochrane, and from that point to use the Timaskaming and Northern Ontario railway down to North Bay, and then the Ontario system of the Grand Trunk. The rumours are to the effect that the section of the Transcontinental east of Cochrane will not be operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific. These rumours have been circulated in Northern Ontario with a view to influencing the electors. The people there have been given to understand 'by people influential with this Government that it is intended to biing tlhe traffic of the Grand Trunk Pacific down to North Day into Ontario, instead of carrying it to the province of Quebec in the summer and to the Maritime provinces in the winter.
Who said that?
I have been told that a good many people have said that, and people very close to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals.
No person ever mentioned it publicly.

The people of Northern
Ontario have been canvassed on the strength of it, and particularly in North Bay. Section 20 of the agreement for the construe-

tkm of a transcontinental railway, which will be found in the statutes of 1903, provides :
When completed the said eastern division shall be leased to, and operated by, the company tor the period of fifty years, at a rental, payable-
The rental is of course provided for. If it is intended and understood that the Grand Trunk Pacific is to operate the whole line, why does the Government feel it necessary to ask Parliament to provide that the Government may take charge of a part of the Transcontinental? If the section had provided that the Government may operate the whole line it would not be so bad, but as it is this legislation fits in absolutely with the rumours which have been so freely circulated. I protest against the section. The Grand Trunk Pacific must in the interests of Canada, and more especially in the interests of Quebec and the Maritime provinces, operate the whole line from Winnipeg to Moncton or no part of it. They must not be allowed to say that they will only go east as far as Cochrane, and then transfer the traffic to the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, and again to the Grand Trunk. I think everybody who has given any thought to this matter will agree that that must not be allowed. Then why does this Government ask Parliament to provide that the Government may operate a part of the line after it is completed? This section does not apply to portions of the line, completed in advance of the completion of the whole line, for that is already provided for in the Acts of 1903 and 1904. This section provides that after the eastern division is completed and until it is leased to the company the whole line or part of it may be operated by the Government. Whoever drew up this Bill must have had in mind that the time might arrive when after the road was completed the Grand Trunk Pacific might say: We are only willing to operate a part of the eastern division, and then the Government could say: Very well, you can operate a portion of the line, and we will operate the rest. We know very well that the Grand Trunk Pacific would choose the portion between Winnipeg and Cochrane.
But what necessity is there for this at all? The Act of 1903 clearly states that the Grand Trunk Pacific are to operate the whole line the moment it is completed. The terms are well defined. The Grand Trunk Pacific are to have the road free of rental for the first seven years, and after that they are to pay rental at the rate of three per cent 306i
on the cost of construction. If the Government have no thought that the Grand Trunk Pacific will refuse to enter upon a lease of the line, why are they providing that the Government may operate the whole or part of this line after it is completed? If the Grand Trunk Pacific are bound to operate the line the moment it is completed, as they are bound to do under the statute, why should the Government ask Parliament to-day for authority to operate a part of the line, which would necessitate the Government's going to great expense in purchasing locomotives, passenger and freight cars, and all the equipment necessary to operate the line with any degree of efficiency. It does seem to me that unless there is something behind this, unless there is some thought that the Grand Trunk Pacific may operate only a portion of the line and that the Government may operate another portion, this legislation is absolutely unnecessary and absolutely without any justification whatever. It only strengthens the position which the Grand Trunk Pacific, take to-day, that they do not know where they are at so far as the operation of the eastern division of the Transcontinental is concerned. That explains why the Grand Trunk Pacific are doing nothing irj the Maritime provinces. It looks as if there was something behind this, and as if the Government were looking forward to excusing the Grand Trunk Pacific from operating the line east of iCoohrane and were going to operate it themselves.

by the Grand Trunk Pacific, and it is not competent to the Grand Trunk Pacific to [DOT]ask for or to insist upon the operation o! that line by their company without operating the whole line. I will not go even a3
far as that; but I understood that he had business affairs which demanded a very large part of his time and attention, land that he might ask to be relieved. We are not asking for his resignation, and I do not want to be understood in that way at all.

There has been a
great deal of discussion in the country as to the attitude of the Government with reference to Major Leonard, and the impression has been conveyed by Government organs that the Government have been wanting to do things in regard to the Transcontinental railway, more particularly in Quebec, which Major Leonard did not approve. The organ of my hon. friend the Postmaster General has discussed Major Leonard very frankly. The organ in Winnipeg of my hon. friend

(Mr. Rogers) has done the same thing. I understood the Premier earlier in the day to say that there was a probability that Major Leonard would retire on account of being interested in private business. The country has naturally been somewhat interested in these articles that have appeared in the Government organs in regard to Major Leonard. In 1912, when the Minister of Railways introduced a measure providing for the retirement of the men who then composed the Transcontinental Commission, we were told that the country was to be congratulated upon the advantage of obtaining the services of Major Leonard, and that it was totally unnecessary to have the four gentlemen, who represented the various portions of the Dominion, dealing with this matter. I was aware, from my knowledge of public affairs, that Mr. Grant, the chief engineer of the Transcontinental, was a man of exceptional ability, and that it was not necessary to add to the engineering side of the management by appointing Major Leonard simply on account of the fact that he was an engineer of experience. The Government, however, decided that it was not wise to have a combination of business men in regard to this matter; they wanted another engineer of experience, and they therefore appointed Major Leonard in place of the other gentlemen of business experience representing the different parts of the country. Eulogies of Major Leonard were pronounced by Conservative organs throughout the country. The special fitness and qualifications he had for the position were set forth in glowing terms by the paid party organs of my hon. friends opposite. The country was to be congratulated upon the fact that, although under the administration of the Liberal party we had, as commissioners, men of experience in business affairs who knew nothing about building a railway, at least we are going to have the right man in the right place. Personally, I somewhat wondered what particular part Major Leonard was going to fill. I felt that he would be a supererogation, seeing that Mr. Grant was there. The Government adopted a rather peculiar attitude in the matter, because they appointed Mr. MacPherson as assistant to the commissioner, although he had no particular qualification for the position except that he was an engineer. This Government assumed the responsibility in 1912, so far as the Transcontinental was concerned, of everything that was done under the direction

of Major Leonard. I had occasion, in a previous discussion in this House, to point out that the present commissioner was responsible for the additional cost, of which hon. gentlemen complained in their federal news bulletin, which has been circulated throughout this country with the ridiculous report which they sent abroad degrading the fair name and financial condition of Canada. These hon. gentlemen said: We have found in Major Leonard a new light, a man in whom the country can have every confidence. The Liberal party spent $97,000,000 on the Transcontinental. Every dollar over and above that has been spent by this Government under the direction of Major Leonard. The Winnipeg Telegram, an organ of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, later deprecated the genius of Major Leonard, and intimated that some mistake had been made in selecting him as the man with the heaven-born qualities who was going to carry this great work to completion. Later on, when it came to be a question of what was to he done in the city of Quebec, when the fine Italian hand of my hon. friend the Postmaster General began to get to work, it was discovered in his particular organ that Major Leonard was not one of those distinguished gentlemen in whom the whole country could have confidence. The organ of my hon. friend the Postmaster General proceeded to attack Major Leonard and declared that he was not the heaven-born commissioner that he was supposed to foe; but that, on the contrary, he stood in the way of carrying out those measures which this wise and economical and all-that-sort-of-thing Government, that sit on the right of the Speaker, wanted to carry out.
Hear, hear.
They admit it.

Yes, they admit it.
We have here under the guise of a measure which assumes that the Transcontinental is going to be finished at the end of the year, a proposition to retire Major Leonard.

That is the object of
the Bill.

That is the sole object of it. Hon. gentlemen may fence; they may finesse; but the fine Italian hand of the Postmaster General is there. Major Leonard stands in the way of the scheme of the Postmaster General in the city of Quebec, and as a consequence my hon. friend has enough influence with this Government to introduce, under this particular, guise, a measure that means that Major Leonard is to be retired, and that his valuable services, so much eulogized three years ago, are no longer to be at the disposal of the country.
That is the proposition that we have here. Hon. gentlemen may disguise it, they may talk about private business interests and they may suggest all kinds of reasons why this should not be, but every one in the province of Quebec will have to hold the Postmaster General responsible for the utterances of his personal organ in regard to this gentleman. My hon. friend from Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) read from the Morning Chronicle of Quebec its opinion of this gentleman. He stands in the way of the desires of the city council of Quebec, and in the way of the views and ambitions of the Postmaster General. It is just as well that the House and the country should understand that Major Leonard, who possessed all the qualifications under the sun which fitted him to be the sole and absolute commissioner of the National Transcontinental railway only two years ago, now, in the estimation of the men who sit on the Treasury benches, does not possess any of those qualifications at all. They say that they made a mistake, that they discovered that Major Leonard has not those qualifications, that he is a man who happens to think for himself, that he happens to exercise those qualifications which hon. gentlemen said he possessed two years ago, and does not propose to be responsible for everything the hon. Postmaster General intends to impose upon this country. Because he has a will of his own and, I assume, is absolutely conscientious in his opinion, because he has those qualifications which hon. gentlemen opposite lauded so highly only a few years ago and because he stands in the way of the peculiar views and ambitions of the Postmaster General, we are having this insidious Bill introduced by means of which Major Leonard is being got rid of. This country is being deprived of his services in order that no longer he may stand in the path of the Postmaster General, and this House is asked to believe that the Transcontinental railway will be absolutely completed within a year, that Major Leonard's services will be no longer required, and that it is proposed to hand the whole control over to the Minister of Railways and Canals.
