On the last occasion when the House was ini Supply, three or four items on page 52 of the Main Estimates were allowed to stand. . There is no reason why, on any of these items, we should not discuss anything that was left undiscussed.

I would suggest that the first item be taken up and then we can have whatever discussion arises.
Railways and Canals-Chargeable to capital * Railways-Intercolonial	railway-Diversion
of line between North Sydney and Leitches Creek, $160,000.

What progress is being made towards the completion of the Halifax and Eastern railway, that is, the branch of the Intercolonial from Dartmouth to Dean Settlement? When will the road be completed and (ready for operation?
My information is that the rails will be laid on the whole of this road, from Dartmouth to Dean, before the end of the current fiscal year.
That is, March next?
Yes.

What weight of rails
aie you putting down?

We are Taking rails from
other parts of the Intercolonial. They run from fifty-six pounds to eighty pounds.
Are you supplying the rails as quickly as they are required by the contractors?
Quite recently they said that they were ready for a few more rails, but up to the present we have been keeping them supplied with all the rails which they require.

I am sorry that
the minister does not anticipate completion of this branch of the Intercolonial railway before the end of March next'. The construction of this road has taken too long entirely. I think the grading is practically completed. I have been informed that the laying of the rails would have been considerably more advanced than it is, were
[Mr. J. D. Reid.l
it not for the fact that the Government have not been supplying rails to the contractors as rapidly as required. I have not made inquiries from official sources into the matter, and possibly I may be in error, but statements to this effect have been made to me from fairly authoritative sources. It has also been remarked to me on many occasions that the rails which the Intercolonial railway is supplying to this branch are altogether too light. I submit that this road, upon which there will be considerable traffic and where the time to be made by passenger trains will be of considerable importance, should have a heavy rail. This road has now been a very long time under construction and I think that its completion should be expedited as much as possible. I think that if a little attention is given to the matter the road should be ready for completion early in the autumn. I should like to ask the minister if that is likely to be the case?

As I have said, we have not heard of any shortage of rails, with the exception of information we received a couple of weeks ago that they were ready for an additional supply. I think, therefore, that my hon. friend must be in error when he says that the completion of the road has been delayed by reason of the shortage of rails.

Will you make
inquiry into the matter?

I certainly will make inquiry, but I am informed by officials of the department that there has been no serious delay up to the present time. I can assure my hon. friend that the completion of this road will not be delayed one moment by reason of any shortage of rails; during the recess rails wild be provided in such a way as to complete the work as speedily as possible. My hon. friend says that the rails are too light.
They are secondhand rails.
Yes, they are taken from parts of the Intercolonial where they are not required and used on the branch line between Dartmouth and Dean.
What is the weight of the rails ?
The average weight is 57 pounds; they run from 56 to 80 pounds.

Are there any 67-pound rails on this branch line ?

Mr. 1REID: Yes, the 67-pound rails are used; they run as high as 80 pounds on this branch. I submit that rails of the weight of 67 or 80 pounds are quite heavy enough for a branch line. I think it is much better to use upon branch lines rails that are not required upon other parts of the line than to place them on the main or through line. I can assure the hon. member that this road will be completed at the earliest possible moment. I understand that the only complaint of the hon. member is that rails are not being promptly supplied in sufficient quantities; if this is his only complaint, there is no reason why the road should not be completed at as early a date as possible.

I should like to impress upon the minister the desirability of urging completion of this road by the contractors at the earliest possible date. When it is in operation it will serve a very considerable section of Halifax county which is now isolated, and it will afford much convenience for a large number of the inhabitants of the district traversed by this line. If the department would display a little more energy in the way of urging completion of the road, I think it could be accomplished at an early date. I would like to ask the minister if at the present time any engineers are making a survey of the Intercolonial railway from Bedford, on the Bedford basin, which is an extension of Halifax harbour, towards Windson junction with a view of securing a better grade from Bedford basin to Windsor junction ?

With reference to the Dartmouth and Dean branch line, I can assure the hon. member that I will take this matter up to-morrow with the contractors and with the department and urge completion at the earliest possible moment. I have received no complaint from the contractor or from any other source, except as I have stated. In the matter of survey parties along the Intercolonial railway, the general manager of Government railways advised me that he had several parties working along the road with a view to having profiles made for the reducing of grades. The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) asked me if a survey party was working in his section; the chief engineer advised me that they are running a line in Cape Britain in connection with the proposed changes in grades on the Intercolonial. I understood him to say also that a survey was being made between Windsor junction
and Bedford in respect of the proposed changes of grade along the Intercolonial in that particular section.
Are any surveys being made between Sydney and East Bay, towards St. Peters, off the line of the Intercolonial railway?

I wired Mr. Gutelius, the
chief engineer, asking him about that and in reply he says that our engineers are running survey lines in Cape Breton in connection with proposed grade revision.

That answer is not to the point because surveys between St. Peters ard Sydney cannot possibly be in connection with grades on the Intercolonial railway unless it is in contemplation to acquire the Cape Breton railway and extend it to Sydney so as to have -a second line on which they can possibly secure better grades.

In making a revision of
grades between Mulgrave and Sydney an alternative route might have to be adopted.
Is this survey being made by Government engineers?
Yes, it is an Intercolonial survey party, in connection with the proposed grade revision.

The minister has informed me, in answer to a question, that a survey party is now endeavouring to relocate the line between Bedford and Windsor Junction for the purpose, I presume, of securing better grades. A very heavy and objectionable grade is found on the Intercolonial railway from Bedford to Windsor Junction. In order to secure this lower grade on the present line of the Intercolonial railway between Bedford and Windsor Junction, I presume the line will have to be lengthened. This brings to my mind a matter which I desire to bring to the attention of the Minister of Railways and which has been frequently suggested in Halifax, particularly by one of its citizens who has given a very careful and considerable study to the matter of railway terminals in that city and vicinity, Mr. Clarence Lon-gard. Mr. Longard, in the press and otherwise, has frequently made the suggestion that in order to secure the shortest line possible to the city of Halifax on the Intercolonial system, and at the same time secure the most favourable gradients ami curvatures, it was desirable to construct a diversion from a point called Wellington on the Intercolonial railway into Dartmouth and, in continuation of this suggestion and as a

part of his project, the construction of a bridge across Halifax harbour from Dartmouth to Halifax, then dealing in some one way, of many suggested, with the question of terminal facilities at Halifax. While this matter has been called to the attention of the Government, I do not think it has received any consideration whatever. I think the suggestion is a very commendable one indeed, and has very considerable merit. It meets with public favour. It is possible to shorten very considerably the mileage of the Intercolonial railway to and from the port of Halifax by constructing the diversion suggested by Mr. Longard. Not only would it shorten the mileage but it would afford very favourable gradients and curvature which is very desirable, because both gradients and curvatures on the Intercolonial railway between Windsor Junction and Halifax are extremely adverse, and I think this is the judgment of all railway men. Apparently it is now proposed to try and secure a better grade, but by lengthening the line. Does the Government favour this idea? Is it the policy of the Government? I think it is possible to shorten the line, and improve the grade at the same time, by constructing the diversion I have just mentioned. From the standpoint of the interests of the port of Halifax it is not desirable to lengthen the Intercolonial. This is easily avoided. I do want to press on the minister the desirability of a careful investigation of Mr. Longard's scheme. The same suggestion was made many years ago by a railway engineer then in the employ of the Government of Canada. The completion of the Halifax and Eastern railway between Dartmouth and Dean's Settlement has created a new situation in respect to the Intercolonial railway on Halifax harbour which demands immediate and very careful attention.. The acting minister wjll perhaps recollect that the western termini of the Halifax and Eastern railway are at Dartmouth. The traffic originating on that line, either freight or passenger, will in most cases be destined for Halifax and therefore it is extremely important that this freight and) passenger traffic should have the easiest access possible to Halifax after reaching Dartmouth. When the Halifax and Eastern railway reaches Dartmouth it, of course, can use the Windsor and Dartmouth branch, trains may proceed from Dartmouth to Windsor Junction, a considerable number of miles, and then proceed to Halifax from Windsor Junction. .
How many miles is it from Dartmouth to Halifax?

I would say
twenty-four or twenty-five miles and it is altogether out of the question to expect passengers to travel that distance in order to get from Dartmouth to Halifax. Of course there is the ferry service between Dartmouth and Halifax, but this hardly affords the requisite facilities. Therefore, I urge upon the Government that preparations be commenced for the construction of a bridge between Dartmouth and Halifax which would enable the Halifax and Eastern Railway trains to reach Halifax over this bridge, and it would also afford opportunity for vehicular and pedestrian travel. The present Minister of Railways promised *me that during 1912 surveys would be made in connection with my suggestion in referring to a railway bridge across Halifax harbour. However, nothing has been done. I do submit that matters have now reached that stage, by reason of the practical completion of the Halifax and Eastern into Dartmouth, that a bridge should be constructed and I want to urge on the minister the urgency and necessity of the early construction of the bridge. Its construction would of course, be a necessity in the event of the adoption of the diversion from Wellington to Halifax via Dartmouth which I have already referred to. The Minister of Public Works did Halifax the honour of a visit last year. He went down there for the purpose of soothing the wounded feelings of the citizens of Halifax at the time the steamers of the Royal Line had been induced by Government influence to move from Halifax to St. John. It was almost necessary for the Minister of Public Works to be in a position to promise the people of Halifax something, so he promised them the early construction of this bridge, a dry-dock and some other things. I have not observed, however, any inclination on the part of the Minister of Public Works to implement the promises he made during that visit, but I want to urge upon him on this occasion in the strongest possible way the necessity for the construction of a railway bridge from Dartmouth to Halifax.
Nearly two years ago, the Minister of Railways announced, in person at Halifax, and with much acclaim, that the Government was about to undertake the construction of additional railway terminals at the port of Halifax. I suppose it was the Gov-

ernment's intention to provide for the port of Halifax the most modern and efficient terminal facilities possible, in order to make it a successful national port for Canadian traffic. I assume it was not the desire of the Government to lengthen the route of the Intercolonial or do anything which would militate against the port as a competitor for export traffic. In connection with the Halifax terminals now under construction, I long ago took the position that before that work was commenced the plans or the general scheme should have been submitted to the best terminal experts available in the world, or at least to men who were experienced as railway terminal engineers; I still incline to that opinion. As time goes on I believe that opposition will steadily grow in Halifax not to the idea }f providing that port with more efficient terminal facilities, but against the method or scheme now proposed for giving the port this terminal accommodation. Under the present scheme the Intercolonial is lengthened very considerably. A railway station is being built at the extreme south end of the city and I cannot help saying- and I think it is the judgment of every citizen of Halifax-that this station is to be very inconveniently located indeed. Much valuable property has been destroyed, and in other respects, which I cannot specifically discuss to-night, irreparable injury done the city. Altogether, I say that the whole project did not receive sufficiently serious consideration from the Government before embarking upon it. I do not think it is yet too late to reflect and reconsider. It is not too late to abandon the present scheme if a better one can be suggested. Many competent persons say this is possible. The whole scheme should have been considered much ,moir>e carefully, and in a broader aspect as well. For instance, I think the construction of a bridge across Halifax .harbour should have been a part of that project. I also think that the relocation and reconstruction of parts of the Intercolonial should have been considered as part of the scheme fbr giving Halifax improved port terminal accommodation. Had these two matters, and there are others doubtless, been taken into consideration when the matter of these terminals was being projected, an altogether different scheme might have been evolved. One much more suitable and convenient in every respect. Even if it were necessary to have terminal facilities at the south end
of the city, where they are now being constructed, and which at least is doubtful, it is quite possible that access by tunnel or otherwise might have been had to that part of the city in another way from that now being employed. Under the present scheme a great deal of valuable property has been taken, and in many other respects, which I do not intend to enlarge upon, the city is being very considerably injured, and I doubt if time will prove the wisdom of the selection of the site for the proposed terminals. Public opinion in Halifax has changed very much. I do not think it is favourable to the present location. I submit the whole matter should be reconsidered and we should have the Government's promise to that effect. If the Government had exercised a little more business acumen in selecting the site for the terminals, and had given less consideration to the political effects, probably things would not be quite just as they are to-day. I trust I have made myself clear to the acting Minister of Railways. First, I desire to impress upon him the importance of a consideration of the relocation of the Intercolonial at points wherever necessary, in order to shorten the line and improve the grade; secondly, the construction of a bridge across Halifax harbour; and lastly a reconsideration of the terminal scheme at Halifax. I should like to hear from the minister upon these points. Will he indicate the Government's views on these matters? I trust the minister will take these matters into his serious consideration at the very earliest opportunity. I am sorry that the short time available to me this evening prevents my discussion of these several matters in a more comprehensive manner.

We have a survey party
between Windsor Junction and Bedford, for the purpose of ascertaining the best way of reducing the grades. They will find out whether that can best be done by reducing the present grades or by an alternative route. The	hon.	member has	advocated	thebuilding of a bridge across the Narrows. When I was in Halifax	some	time	agoI remember that when I asked about certain old wooden piers in the harbour there, I was	told	that there	had	been	abridge across the Narrows. I agree with	the	hon. member	that	a bridge
would be a good thing and more particularly now that the Dartmouth and Deans branch railway is being built. But the Government have undertaken a large number of works

at Halifax; they are spending a great deal of money on these works and in addition there is the amount being expended on the Dartmouth and Deans branch. It is impossible to do everything in one year. As soon as the road is completed, or is nearing completion, this matter should be taken up. The hon. gentleman says it is twenty-four miles from Dartmouth to Halifax around by the railway. That must entail great expense in the carriage of freight as compared with what it would cost, if by the construction of a bridge across the harbour, it was cut down to probably a mile. I must take issue with the hon. member in so far as the plans of Halifax harbour are concerned. The hon. gentleman does not agree with the plans and layout but these matters are left to men who have had large experience in this kind of work. It is not to be expected that even the Minister of Railways and Canals., or my hon. friend who has not had experience, would be qualified to come to the best conclusion as to the layout and work necessary to make Halifax one of the finest harbours in the world.
How much does the minister propose to spend on the terminals at Halifax?
It is difficult to say for the reason that the terminals at Halifax will be proceeded with as they are required.
The plans are completed, I understand, and the contracts let.

The plans are completed and I have a photograph here showing what the works will look like when they are finished. The whole plan provides for several new berths for steamers and at the present time there is a contract for about 2,000 feet of piers and two berths. That work is under contract and when it is completed no doubt the work will be extended from time to time as further accommodation is required.

Has the minister no
figures to show how much he proposes to spend upon improvements at that port?
I have the figures of the contracts we have let.

How much do they
amount to?
The total amount of the contracts let will be $6,500,000.
Does that cover the whole of the proposed expenditure?
The station is not included in that.
There must be an estimate of the whole layout.

I have no. estimate of the
whole layout or of what may be required in,years to come. I have an estimate of the works that are let.

In the department over which I had the honour formerly to preside, when any particular layout was designed and the plans prepared, just as in the case of Halifax harbour, there was always an estimate of the engineers showing what would be the total outlay. My hon. friend must have that information in his department.

Take Montreal harbour, for
example. We all know that there are so many berths or piers laid out and that an estimate is made for a series of piers. At Halifax an estimate has been made of the works that we have under contract and that is all that will be required for some little time. When we get that work completed we can provide for another series of berths if required.

My hon. friend from
New Glasgow (Mr. Sinclair) asked what was the estimated cost of the total layout. The Montreal Harbour Commissioners have plans prepared and although the work may extend over a number of years, and they do not propose to let contracts in the meantime, they still have an estimate of the total cost.
We have an estimate of the work we proposed to do at the present time.
Have you not made an estimate of the other?

No, that is all that is required and, as I stated, the total estimated cost is $6,500,000. When that work is completed, or nearly completed, if we wish to extend it, we will have another estimate made and new contracts called for.

How many ships can
;ou accommodate with the work you are proposing now?

We have six slips provided
for in the contract that is now let.

You have berths with
sufficient accommodation for six steamers?
No, six piers.

Whai is the length of
the piers?
1,200 feet.
That would give accommodation for four times as many vessels.

Yes, and if required the
work will be extended.
Does the estimate include the breakwater?
Neither the breakwater nor the station is included in this estimate of $6,500,000.

Does the department
not intend to construct a breakwater?

Yes, but it is not in the
present contract. We have not let a contract for the breakwater or the station.

Might I have
some intimation from the minister that he will direct that a survey he made of this relocation I suggest between Wellington station. and Dartmouth during the present season?
All right.

When you are
equipping a port in a modern fashion for national ia.s well as local purposes, it is desirable to have the line of railway as short as possible and with the most favourable gradients and curvatures. Will the minister also inform me if it is the intention of the Government to construct a railway station in the north end of the city of Halifax or if it is their intention to allow the present station to remain for certain purposes or whether they are to remove that and have a new station at the south end of the city alone where the terminals are being located?

I agree with the hon. member that the line of railway between Wellington and Halifax should be as short as possible, and I will certainly give instructions that a survey be made during the present year between Dartmouth and Wellington for the purpose of having any changes made that are necessary in order to shorten the railway and to improve the gradients and curvatures.

After having made that survey and after having taken into consideration the construction of the bridge, the Railway Department might find that they can provide terminal facilities without the carrying out of the terminal project in the way they now propose doing. While it might be considered desirable to
construct piers at the south end of the city, where they are now about to be constructed, the piers might be approached in a different way altogether without the amount of injury being done to the city and private property that will be done if the present project is carried out in its entirety. What about the railway station?

I agree with the hon. member. In order, however, that the suggestion of the hon. member may be taken into consideration, I shall to-morrow forward a letter to those in charge of the terminals and the general manager of the road in order that they may give consideration to the suggestions of the hon. member with reference to that survey.
With reference to the stations, that matter has not, so far as I am aware, been considered. The contract has been let for the main terminals, but nothing further has been decided upon by the Railway Department or the general manager. That matter will be considered at a later date.

Some time ago I asked the minister the following question with reference to the Dartmouth to Dean Settlement branch that is being constructed:
If the said original contract has been sublet, what are the names of the sub-contractors and the mileage allotted to each, and the amounts payable to said sub-contractors under the contracts sublet to them, as aforesaid?
The answer was:
The original contract has not been sublet.
Every one in Nova Scotia knows that not only was it sublet, but it was sublet two or three times. It was sublet first to an Italian firm by the name of Cavicci and Pagani, who sublet it again to a number of other contractors. I was surprised to get this answer from the Minister of Railways, and it shakes my faith in the accuracy of his information as to what is going on in his department. I thought this a suitable time, when we are dealing with the question of Halifax, to ask my hon. friend whether he has any more information than he had when he answered this question about a month ago. He certainly was misinformed when he said that the original contract to Mr. M. P. Davis had not been sublet.

There is a clause in these contracts that the contractor has not the right to sublet without the consent of the minister. No application has been made to the Railway Department by the contractor for

its consent to his subletting the contract, and we have no knowledge of this contract being sublet to the firm mentioned or to any one else. The estimates come in from the engineer in charge of the work every month in the name of the contractor Davis. We send a cheque to Davis; and there is nothing in any way, shape or form on record in the department to show that these men are sub-contractors of Davis. Davis may be employing the men to do the work for him, not as sub-contractors-
They are sub-contractors.

They may be; but Davis may have such an arrangement that they are not really considered as sub-contractors and therefore it may not have been necessary to make application for the acceptance of them as such.
The minister knows that the work is not being done by Davis or directly tinder his control?

I think the hon. member will agree that, unless an application has been made to the department or some information given to it, that they are sub-contractors, and as long as the work is proceeded with, we cannot consider-

The firm of M. P.
Davis have never been in charge down there at all.

They might not be on the
work, but they can hire a foreman to do the work.

If my hon. friend will
look into the matter, he will find they have turned the contract over to the subcontractors and have kept a ten per cent rake-off themselves, just as has been done in other cases.

Has the minister made any rearrangement of the suburban railway service between Halifax and Windsor junction? He will remember this was a matter of much discussion at Halifax during last winter, and I referred to the matter myself one day during this session. The service at present in force is very unsatisfactory. I was advised by the minister on one occasion that some time in the spring or early summer a new time-table would be issued. Is it likely to be issued soon?

The general manager was
here about a week ago; and I made inquiry of him as to the suburban service both at

St. John and at Halifax, because there was some complaint last winter with reference to both places. He assured me that there were no complaints; that everything was apparently satisfactory. At all events I have not received any complaints. since last February. I do not know whether the hon. member has heard of any of late or not. In so far as the suburban services at Halifax and St. John are concerned, they must be in a fair state, because no comp'aints are being made to the department at the present time.

I do not suppose the
people can go on complaining forever. To be frank, I must admit that, within the past few days, I have not heard of any complaints msyselli|, nor have any been conveyed to me, nor have I seen any made in the public press; but I can safely say that the suburban service given during all last winter was very unsatisfactory, and there was no goo-d reason for discontinuing the former service which had been in force for a great number of years.
I think the summer timetable is now effective, and that everything is perfectly satisfactory.
Have you fixed up the St. John suburban service satisfactorily?
I think that was fixed up in February.
The people are worn out with making complaints.

I think the hon. member is not fair in making that statement because, when I was at St. John last February, I met a deputation who were all agreed at that time that the service was perfectly satisfactory with the arrangement I then made with them.

'All agreed.' That is
a few Conservative workers.

At that meeting a subcommittee was appointed to meet me and discuss the matter, and the hon. member will know if he read the papers at the time that that committee was composed of about half Liberals and half Conservatives. We arranged a time-table that was perfectly satisfactory. The Liberals of the city themselves wired to Mr. Hazen that they were perfectly satisfied with the arrangements made at the time. From the information I have had since, I am led to believe that there is not the slightest complaint about the suburban service at St. John.

I hope it is entirely
satisfactory. Of course, there is a great difference between the service in summer and in winter. It is the winter service they were complaining of more particularly. I may say that the people generally were well pleased at the reception that the minister gave them-they were delighted with his affability, and he promised to remove the difficulties and they were in hopes that great improvement would be made. I heard that the suburban cars were old cars, frequently heated with coal-stoves and lighted with old-fashioned oil lamps, giving a wretched service, and such accommodation as we used to have on the Intercolonial thirty or forty years ago. The people could not imagine that they could be so treated. Why was it that this suburban service had been satisfactory for so many years under Mr. Blair, Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Graham, and that this dissatisfaction occurred so recently? Prior to freight trains coming into Hampton there was no dissatisfaction with the suburban trains.

I arranged a service, and abandoned the idea of the use of passenger cars on the freight train. After that, as I understood, the complaints ceased. On March 16 the hon. member for North Cape Breton moved :a resolution in this House with regard to Intercolonial branch lines. At that time I desired to make a few remarks, but I could not do so on account of my failure to secure a copy of a report for which I moved over a year ago, during the last session. At that time, on March 16 the Minister of Railways suggested to me that I would have an opportunity of discussing this question when his Estimates were under consideration and for a few moments I desire to discuss the proposed line of railway from Orangedale to Cheticamp in the county of Inverness. I would have much preferred making these observations earlier in the session and would have done so were it not for the refusal of the hon. Minister of Railways to place on the table of the House the report which I have referred to.
Since I first had the honour of a seat in this House I have taken every opportunity to place before the Minister of Railways and the Government the importance of the construction of this line from the standpoint of a traffic gatherer for the Intercolonial railway, and the development of the natural wealth of the country through which it passes. In 1911 the late Ministry assured me that if my statements were borne out by the report of accredited engineers, they would undertake the construction of this road in 1912. It may be supposed that, on account of this occurring very close to the date of an election, the assurance then made by the Ministry was

a pre-election promise, but I may say that at that time an election was not anticipated. The -Government had no intention of going to the country untii late in 1912. Besides, the history of railway promises in Inverness county for twenty years previous to 1897 was such that repeating similar promises in 1912 would not be calculated to be .received very favourably by the people of that county. My knowledge of these facts convinced me that it would not be the part of good judgment for me even to publicly refer during the campaign of 1911 to the assurances I got from my party that the construction of this road would be undertaken in 1912, and I absolutely avoided ever referring to the subject publicly during that campaign. I refer to this matter particularly at the present time, because if the present Government fail to construct this road I hope to keep the promise fresh in the minds of the Liberal party, members of which assured me that construction of this road would be undertaken, and that this promise will be redeemed when they come into power which, according to all indications, will not be in the distant future.
I am going to attempt to convince you, Mr. Chairman, 'and the acting Minister of Railways that the proposed line of railway from Orangedaie to Chetieamp is one of the most promising and really meritorious proposed branch lines of the Intercolonial [DOT]that has 'ever been discussed in this House, .both as a supplier of traffic to the Intercolonial railway and as a means for industrial development.
I wish first to refer to the many prospective sources of traffic along this route. I think I can say in a general way that that section of the country from Orangedaie to Chetieamp is one of the most wealthy of its size in eastern Canada.
Tlie country abounds in valuable minerals, lumber. The coast waters teem with first-class commercial fish, and, the agricultural possibilities of the country from Orangedaie to Chetieamp are enormous. I shall first refer briefly to some of the mineral deposits to be found along the line and at close proximity to it the development of which would be assured by the construction of this line.
At a distance of about six miles from Orangedaie, the southern terminus of the proposed line, there are very large deposits of silica. This silica has been developed only recently; a company has been incorporated for the purpose of manufacturing it into its commercial products. This com-

pany applied to the Legislature of Nova Scotia recently for a charter to construct a railway from their properties to the Intercolonial railway. The line follows the route of the proposed branch line from Orange-dale to Chetieamp, and if the Government undertakes the construction of this road, the necessity of the company's building this branch railroad from their property to Orangedaie will be removed and their goods would be carried over the proposed Orange-dale-Oieticamp line. The manufacture of silica into its various commercial products by this company would contribute very largely to traffic upon the Intercolonial railway. Some three miles farther north, very valuable deposits of dolomite have been discovered. That enterprising concern, the Dominion Iron -and Steel Company, made a thorough examination of these deposits, and as a result they have purchased the property. In order to obtain accurate information on the subject I wrote to one of the leading officials of that company and received a reply, of which the following is a part :
As the properties mentioned above, however, are only get-at-able by water for shipping purposes and as there is always a demand for stone fresh from the quarry during the Winter season, I have no doubt but a railway would develop a business of from 250 to 500 tons a day over this line.
The winter season, therefore, is the time when the traffic would be the greatest. The Dominion Iron and Steel Company get their dolomite from Newfoundland and Marble Mountain in the county of Inverness, and they can get it only during the summer months, during open navigation. This mine at Whycocomagh, which is on the proposed line, could be operated in the winter time, and that is the season during which the Dominion Iron and Steel Company -are unable to get their dolomite from the other two sources to which I have referred. I anticipate that with the growth and development of this property, not 500 tons but 5,000 tons a day would be carried over this route. The property has been subjected to a very careful examination and the quality of the mineral has been found to be first-class.

Cheticamp, were it not- that they were anxious to get hold of the coal deposits at Ste. Rose and Chimney Comer. I still adhere to that opinion. I am firmly of that opinion. We come now to other important mineral deposits. You may be amazed to know that such a quantity of valuable mineral can be found in the county of Inverness and that these minerals are still undeveloped. I charge against Mackenzie and Mann the fact that these mineral properties have not been developed. I am convinced that as far as developing the resources of the county of Inverness are concerned the greatest curse that ever befel the county was the entrance therein of Mackenzie and Mann. I will admit that they have developed their own coal property, and that that has been a great blessing to the county of Inverness, but that is only a drop in the bucket as compared with the industrial development that would result in the opening up of our various mineral deposits throughout the county. If that line through the county of Inverness had been owned by the Government, or by any unselfish corporation, the road would have been extended to Cheticamp long ago and the properties that I have referred to would have been developed. In that sense I say that the advent of Mackenzie and Mann has been a curse to the county of Inverness.
I now desire to refer to the gypsum properties in Inverness. Gypsum is regarded by many people ae a low priced mineral, which is difficult to be economically handled except under the most favourable condition for mining and transportation, but the gypsum industry in that part of Nova Scotia is destined to become a very important one. In the county of Inverness, through the energy and business acumen of the late Rev. Father Fiset, of Cheticamp, a very valuable plant has been erected there and gypsum is being manufactured. The value of the manufactured product ranges from $7 to $12 a ton. It will be seen from this that the gypsum industry in North Inver-

ness is destined to assume very great proportions the moment we have proper transportation facilities. While this mineral as found in nature is low priced it becomes valuable in manufactured form, and is in great demand-the market of which is daily on the increase. The Great Northern Mining Company have operated their plant for the last few years. A delegation from that concern waited upon the Government in 1912. They expressed their readiness to enter into a contract with the Government to supply this proposed railway with a certain number of cars of manufactured gypsum a day at a fixed price which appears to me at least to be a very paying rate. I refer to that to show the great necessity for transportation facilities in so far as this article is concerned. I desire to read a communication which was sent to the Government by the manager of the Great Northern Mining Company and which is as follows:
Ottawa, 30th January, 1912. Honourable Prank Cochrane,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa, Can.
Honourable Sir,
Complying with your request made on the occasion of our interview of the 26th instant regard ng the building of a branch line of the Intercolonial railway from Orangedale to Cheticamp, we beg to submit the following as an inducement to procure the building of said line:
(1)	We shall give the railway the importation of all our supplies (bags, barrels, hair, retarder, coal, oil, machinery, etc.), and we shall export by said railway from six to seven carloads of manufactured gypsum every day for the Montreal and Quebec markets; and as our trade shall increase we shall also ship a considerable amount to the intermediate towns on the line.
(2)	We are also willing to enter into an agreement with the Government to pay $3.75 per ton from Cheticamp to Montreal for every ton of manufactured gypsum, our company will ship over the road within the period of five years. This rate includes the established charge of three dollars from Mulgrave to Montreal and seventy-five cents from Cheticamp to Mulgrave, which latter rate, if reckoned for the whole distance to Montreal, would amount to the enormous freight rate of over $8 per ton. But in order that this offer will be binding on ourselves, we desire the Government to take immediate action and at least to grant sufficient money to insure a survey of said line next season.
Your Government will readily understand that, in order to bond ourselves to this generous offer we must have a reasonable assurance of the time the Government proposes to have said line completed so that we may not be embarrassed in making our exportation contracts in the meantime.
Great Northern Mining and Railway Co.,
Limited, Hubert Aucoin.
Managing Director.
This will show you the importance to this concern of the construction of the road. This is only one of half a dozen similar concerns which would start operations in this part of the country if they only had means of transportation. They have an unlimited market for 'their product in the cities of Canada. The unfortunate part is that they cannot hope to do any large amount of business while they have their present means of transportation. They are greatly discouraged and you can hardly blame them. By this communication you will see that the Great Northern Mining Company are willing to supply this proposed line with six or seven cars of manufactured gypsum a day, and that is only one-sixth of the amount of gypsum freight that would be carried over this line. The gypsum found in the county of Inverness has been subjected to a very exacting examination and analysis and it has been pronounced the best quality of any gypsum found in Canada. As a result the product, when manufactured, secures good prices, such as assure the manufacture in increasing quantities.
I now desire to refer to another important industry and that is the fishing industry. We have located off the county of Inverness the most valuable fishing grounds perhaps in eastern Canada. Off of the county of Inverness the fleets of the United States and of western Nova Scotia secure a large portion of their catch every year. Since the very first settlement of the county of Inverness the fishing industry has been one of the' very greatest importance. It has been carried on successfully until recent years. I might point out that one hundred and thirty years ago a firm from the Channel islands came over to Cheticamp, erected a fishing establishment there and they have continued doing a splendid business and are found there to-day, one of the most prosperous concerns of this kind in Nova Scotia.
I refer to that as an indication of the value of the fishing industry in that part of the country. I am sorry to say that in recent years, on account of the fresh fish market having secured the greater portion of our fish, in consequence of the better prices paid in those markets, and in consequence of relieving the fishermen of a great deal of the work they had to do and the expense they had to incur in their old method of curing fish, the people of North Inverness have been discouraged because they have not been able to place the products of their labour on the fresh fish market. We are eighty miles away from the nearest Intercolonial railway station, and it would be

markets; this would give a market at home for the products of our. farms, and would give such a stimulus to the agricultural industry in that portion of the country as the farmers there have never engaged in. Without a railway, there is only one thing, in my judgment, that will happen, namely that the country will rapidly become depopulated. In fact, our young .men are leaving it every day. They cannot remain there, because they cannot carry on the farming industry under present conditions of labour and make it pay. Our farmers must meet the increased cost of production and at the same time are not permitted to enjoy the conveniences enjoyed by the farmers in other parts of the country more favourably circumstanced with respect to markets and transportation conveniences.
This line also runs through a lumber region, hard and soft lumber being found in large quantities. This portion of the country has never been exploited so far as lumber is concerned, although there are large quantities of very valuable lumber such as pit timber, which finds a very ready market close at home in the mines of Sydney and Inverness. Very fine qualities of hard wood are found all along this proposed route at varied distances from the line, which would find ready market. With a railway this valuable property could be placed upon the markets, and the country would become more wealthy as a result. This lumber is absolutely valueless to-day for lack of transportation.
I desire briefly to refer to the prospective tourist trade of the proposed Orangedale-Cheticamp branch line. This trade has increased to an almost startling degree in many countries of recent years. An article published in the American Review of Reviews in 1907 places the annual income of France from this traffic at $500,000,000, and of Italy -at $100,000,000. The same article places the expenditure of the American tourist in England at $25,000,000 a year. During the past five years, this trade has greatly increased, so that the above figures are much lower than the -amounts now spent. Other statistics show that Switzerland's annual income from tourists amounts to $150,000,000. According to the United States statistics, the state of Florida gets a larger revenue from this trade than fro-m the products of the soil; an-d tourists spend $7,000,000 each year in the Adirondacks, and at least $40,000,000 in the pine woods of the state of M-aine. The President of the
[Mr. A- W. Chisholm.'
American Civic Federation, in a speech in September last, estimated that the American spent abroad in 1910 the startling amount of $350,000,000.
I think it is conceded that Canada is endowed by nature with more natural attractions for the tourist than any other country on the g-l-obe. I fear though that enough is not being done by this -country to develop this trade. I have always felt that the Government of this country have neglected their opportunities in this respect, particularly .in so far as the Maritime provinces -are concerned. Any enterprising railw-ay concern owning and operating the Intercolonial railway would, I am convinced, regard it as their first duty, from a business standpoint, to fully advertise the many tourist attractions to be found in the country through which this road passes, would build up-to-date hotels, thoroughly protect our fresh water fisheries and game, of which we have abundance, and in every possible way promote and encourage tourist traffic.
I feel I am correct when I -say that this railway line from Whycocomagh to Cheti-camp passes through a country with greater attractions than any other part of *eastern Canada of its size. For boating *and bathing Whycocomagh c-annot be surpassed. The angler can satisfy his desires *to his heart's content, not in one but in a *half dozen streams flowing into Whycoco-*magh bay and lake Ainslie. Trout Brook, I venture to say, has not its equal in the *Maritime provinces as a trout angling stream. The Margaree river is long known *as the best salmon angling river in Nova Sootia. The Margaree and Trout Ibrook *attracts many tourists every year, but on account of their distance from the nearest Tailw.ay, only a small number visit these waters now, as compared with the many who would take advantage of the great angling here afforded, if they could get to *and from here by rail. Little river in Cheticamp is another beautiful fresh water *river, where salmon abounds, and where 'angling is most successfully carried on. 'The scenery all along this route is unsurpassed for beauty and grandeur. In fact, the only thing required to bring thousands *of summer tourists to Inverness county is railway conveniences, and there is no reason why we could not capture our share of this ever-increasing traffic possessing as we do so many tourist attractions unsurpassed by any other country in *the world.

I have great faith in the extent of the tourist trade which can be developed in this portion of the country. I wish the acting Minister of Railways could find time to drive along this route from Orangedale to Oheticamp and through the beautiful country of Whycocoimagh, Lake Ainslie and the Margarees. I am sure he would say that the possibilities of the tourist traffic there are almost unlimited and would he moved to immediate activity in an effort to give the tourist of the world an insight into the many and varied attractions which are found all along this proposed route.
Another important matter which I desire to .bring to the notice of the House is that Cheticamp is within forty miles of a very populous portion of the province of Quebec, the Magdalen islands. The Magdalen islands are now served by a steamer running from Pictou, a distance of 130 miles. I have the assurance of mariners that the waters are open much later in the fall of the year between Cheticamp and the Magdalen islands than between Pictou and the Magdalen islands. If this line of railway were constructed, a daily mail could be given to the people of the Magdalen islands and a much more satisfactory connection with the rest of the world. The people of that portion of Quebec are as much interested in the construction of the line from Orangedale to Cheticamp as are the people of Inverness county. I am sure that if the hon. member for Gaepe (Mr. GauthieT) were here this evening he would give me his hearty support. These islands have a population of over 7,000 all of whom are most interested in being brought into closer connection with the main land. This Government and the Government of Nova Scotia are paying $15,000 a year in steamship subsides to steamers plying along the coast of Inverness, this being the means of travel and transportation enjoyed at present by the inhabitants of the northern portion of the county. There would be absolutely no necessity for this expenditure if this line were constructed. This may appear a small matter; but if you capitalize this amount, which is paid out every year, it is worth $375,000, which amount would go a long way in the construction of this road. All these facts contribute to one end, and that is the justification for the construction of this portion of the road. I have endeavoured to point out the probable traffic " that could be
gathered by this line of road. I think that hon. members who have listened to me will adlmit that, while I am not making any effort at rhetoric, at least I give every indication of being fair in my representation of this case. The hon. gentlemen who have listened to me must be astounded that all this wealth has been left undeveloped up to this time, but I have given you the reason why, in my judgment, this is the case and that is that the pioneer railway builders in the county, Mackenzie & Mann have since their advent into the county acted the dog in the manger, and did not hesitate to sacrifice all other considerations, so far as Inverness is concerned, in their effort to get control of the mineral wealth of the county.
"Now I wish to say a word or two with regard to the probable cost of the construction of this road. .It will be said, and I think I was told by the Minister of Railways, that the solution of the railway difficulties in the county of Inverness could be met by the construction of the Inverness railway northward. I do not agree that the extension of the Inverness railway to Cheticamp would be calculated to develop our resources. That road if extended north would serve the' coal mines, but the experience of the Port Hood coal mining company and the Mabou coal mining company with Mackenzie and Mann was not likely t<5 encourage capitalists to invest in the development of the coal mines at Ste. Rose and Chimney Corner. The Mabou and Port Hood mines have closed down. As far as the Mabou mine is concerned I think a great portion of the difficulty can be attributable to the fact that it was practically impossible to get any reasonable transportation agreement with Mackenzie and Mann. It was because of these difficulties that I was led to ask the Government to include this system in the schedule in order to bring it under the operation of the Railway Commission. If that had been done Mackenzie and Mann would have had to submit to the findings of that court. At present they can carry on their operations to suit themselves. I have said that I do not think that the solution of the railway difficulties of the county of Inverness will be found in the extension of the Inverness line north. The silica property, the barytes property, and the petroleum property would not be on that line. That large and prosperous section of country 'from Orangedale to 8. W. Margaree would not be served by the extension of the Inverness Railway north and could never hope to get railway conveniences if that road were extended north. The resources of that portion of the county could not be developed. Whereas the Orangedale-Cheti-camp road would serve the whole country from Orangedale to Cheticamp. The experience of the people of Inverness with the Inverness Railway and Coal Company has been such as to discourgage them. There is not the slightest hope from that railway company. The people realize that if the development of the country's resources depends on Mackenzie and

Mann's road, it will remain as at present until Mackenzie and Mann get hold of them all, as they ATe thying to do with the properties at Ste. Rose and Chimney Corner. I think I have submitted to the acting Minister of Railways sufficient information to justify his regarding this as one of the most important proposed branch lines in connection with the Intercolonial railway. I would suggest that he be not so ready to lose faith in the findings of his engineers as was the Minister of Railways. I regret that when I asked the Minister of Railways in the House last year what his opinion was of the report of Mr. Tessier, he told me that in his judgment the report was too rosy and would not be borne out by the facts. I am sure that if the hon. Minister of Railways were well acquainted with the facts he would not have made that assertion. The statements which I have made to-night are absolutely correct, and I submit should be ample to satisfy the most exacting of requirements of the hon. minister if he desires to mete out to the people of Inverness that measure of fair and just treatment which they will merit. If the minister desires to supplement the information which he now has, I would suggest to him that he send one or two engineers into the county of Inverness with instructions to look over the whole situation. I may point out to him though that the sending of engineers there before an election, was to the people of Inverness a veritable emetic, in view of the experience of that period before the Inverness railroad was constructed. Again, if he will go from Orangedale to Cheticamp, he will find the many sources of traffic to which I have referred. I believe that the Minister of Railways is a business man, and if he takes a business-like view of this situation; if he sends his engineers down there, and if he starts with the premises that the road will be constructed if the conditions justify such construction, I am satisfied that the road will be constructed without delay. Let me in closing assure the hon. minister that the people-of Inverness are grateful and if this Government will give our people the relief that the construction of the Orangedale-Cheticamp line would surely give, they will secure a warm spot in the memory of a grateful and warm hearted people.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Inverness, and I certainly feel that that part of the county should receive consideration at the earliest possible moment. I read the report made by the

engineer; I certainly felt that it was very rosy, and wondered why the Inverness Railway Company did not extend their road through that part of the county if the results would have been as suggested in the report and by my hon. friend. However, at this late hour all I can say is that that section of the country is the same in respect of which some other parties called upon me and urged the completion of this road. I think I stated that the chief engineer of the Intercolonial railway would look over the district during the coming season, and I shall urge upon the general manager that that be done.
As we sat until about four o'clock this morning, I would suggest that, if it is agreeable, we pass an item or two and adjourn. I will bring the Estimates on some time to-morrow, when any further discussion that is desired may take place.

There has been no change, the policy as laid down by the minister will be adhered to. The hon. member for St. John asked a question on the 29th of May as to what effort had been made to have the -Grand Trunk take over that section of the National Transcontinental railway between Moncton and Edmundston. That was answered by the Prime Minister to-day in this discussion. The hon. gentleman wanted me to bring down any correspondence between the Government or the commission and the Grand Trunk Pacific. There is no correspondence; any communication so far as the Government was concerned, was verbal discussion between the Minister of Railways and the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The right hon. leader of the Opposition asked me to state the condition of the road between Quebec and Edmundston. I may say that the part between Quebec and Edmundston is completed; the only remaining contractors on the road between Quebec and Moncton is the firm of M. P. and J. T. Davis, and they inform me that between Quebec and mile 150 there is between 50,000 yards of train-haul filling and 30,000 yards of ballasting to be done; 20,000 ties have to be replaced and there is a little fencing and six miles of track in Monk yard. The work will be all completed by the 1st of August next.

Will the Government continue the practice which has been followed of shipping materials and men to Hudson bay, using lumber and vessels and all that kind of thing and throwing away public money ? Would it not be better to give a contract to some large and responsible firm of contractors who are accustomed to establishing termini and let them take charge of the whole work. Last year the work in Hudson bay was being done by day labour, and I understand that men away up in that north country were only paid for the days they worked. You can see the difficulties that would arise under those conditions. But as it is the Government are squandering the public money and not getting any further ahead with this work.

I am glad the hon. member has called attention to the Hudson Bay railway because I see in the Evening Citizen to-night an item with reference to work in the construction of the Hudson Bay railway which, so far as 1 know, is absolutely false and untrue. The article refers to the conditions of work on the railway from Le Pas north. It
12 m. speaks of the cruel treatment of men by the contractors. Of course, the Government are dealing only with the contractors, and so far as we are *concerned no charge has been laid or made to the department. Mr. McArthur and I think Mr. Boyd are the contractors and I believe that there are no better contractors in Canada, and no men who would treat their men better. We made contracts last year for taking the necessary material and men to Hudson bay. Ships were chartered to the very best advantage. It is true that a couple of vessels met with mishap, one got into Nelson and if it had not been for the captain's own fault the vessel could have been discharged without loss. However, they were insured and the Government will not lose by the accidents that did happen. That was the only way to get the material to Hudson bay, and the Government are making similar arrangements to take up the necessary supplies and materials for the work.

And you have it
done by day's work?
Yes, in charge of one of our best engineers. There is no reason why our own engineers and staff should not be able to do the work as cheaply as contractors.
No good.

I am satisfied that if we were doing it by contract the hon. member would make just about as strong a speech as he has done, censuring us for letting a contract on account of the high rate we would have to pay.

The department bought
two boats from Poison's.

They are going up to
Nelson this summer. We found that we could buy a steamer for what it would cost to charter it for two trips and so we bought these two vessels. Some other time I would be glad to discuss this matter with the hon. member for Pictou and give him more information.

I do not expect to have another opportunity this session of discussing the matter with my hon, friend. I want to tell him that the Government are simply throwing away their money, absolutely squandering it by their present methods. They have been pottering around Hudson bay for two years but nothing has been done yet. They sent up a gang of useless heelers from the Maritime provinces-	.
I did not think you had any. heelers in Nova Scotia.

My hon. friend's party has. That is all they have done, and they did not even gain any political advantage by that for every one of the men they took up came down mad at the way they had been treated. If the Government are really earnest about this project, they should give the job to a big firm of contractors accustomed to do work of this kind. The minister will go on again this year fooling away with the situation, and when the people get at this Government they will throw them out of power and find that the only results attained have been to put money into the hands of a few people.
We will have it on our hands.

If my hon. friend
was gaining some political advantage by it, I would speak with some degree of feeling, but it is not so. In the Maritime provinces we know more about the situation than do the people of central Canada. The people of Ontario and Quebec have nothing to do with Hudson bay, commercially or otherwise. The men in Manitoba

have to do with it by reason of the fact that they are interested in the construction of the railway, but Nova Scotia is the most interested. All the supplies come from our province and so do the men. A story of the most pitiful government mismanagement that ever occurred in any country could be told of the way this Government have handled this project. Why does not the minister take hold of the situation, and have these terminals built? If he goes on pottering away with it this summer we shall be no further ahead at the end of the year, and no doubt there will be a lot Of lumber floating around Hudson bay with nobody to look after it.

There was one vessel
that attracted my attention-the Alcazar. She took a cargo of hard pine from some American port, came to Halifax and from there went to Hudson bay, came back to Halifax, and then went to North Sydney with her full cargo.
Only part of the cargo.

A fairly full cargo. I
imagine that this is rather an expensive w'ay of getting hard pine to Hudson bay. There is no reason why this hard pine should not ask for another ride around the gulf this year. The Alcazar's cargo of lumber is now piled alongside the Intercolonial at North Sydney, and I would like to know what the minister is going to do with it. Will we be able to buy it for kindling wood at North Sydney, or is it to be put on board the Alcazar again?

We are going to take it back again to Hudson bay. The Alcazar's captain, on account of the poor unloading facilities and the lateness of the season, feared that he might not be able to get, out of the bay again, and that is why the cargo was not discharged. I do not believe there would have been any danger if he had remained a little longer. We are sending the lumber up again this summer, and I hope this time it will stay there.

Will you guarantee
it will not be back again at North Sydney in the autumn?

Yes.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
With the permission of
the House, I would like to read further
messages which have been received respecting the disaster to the Empress of Ireland:
From Mr. Harcourt to the Governor General.
London, 1st June, 1914.
Please transmit to Prime Minister following message received to-day from "Government of New South Wales. Begins:-New South Wales shocked at enormous sacrifice of valuable human lives in Empress of Ireland disaster; wish you favour by conveying to bereaved relatives on behalf of Government and people of this sister British Dominion profound sorrow and sympathy.
(Sgd) Harcourt.
From Mr. Harcourt to the Governor General.
London, 1st June, 1914.
Following telegram has been received from Governor General of Australia:
Please convey Australia's deepest sympathy with Canada in terrible maritime disaster which has brought sorrow to so many homes in the sister Dominion.
( Sgd) Harcourt.
Dunedin, June 3rd, 1914.
Honourable R. L. Borden,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Citizens of Dunedin desire to express sincere sorrow at deplorable disaster and condolence with bereaved.
Shacklock,
Mayor.
May 30th, 1914.
Sir,-With deep feeling of sorrow I learn of the terrible disaster of the fine ship ' Empress of Ireland,' which envelopes with, grief this beautiful country.
In the name of the sons of Cuba residing ill this country, and in my own, as the representative of the Republic on this Dominion, I beg to extend to the Canadian people, through you, the testimony of our most sincere regrets.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
N. Perez Stable,
Consul General for Cuba in Canada. The Right Hon. Robert L. Borden,
Premier of Canada,
Ottawa.
Clifton Hotel, Niagara Falls, Ont.,
June 2, 1914.
His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught:
The Mexican Government has instructed us in a cable received this morning to express to your Royal Highness and to the people of Canada the sincere condolence of the Mexican nation for the bereavement suffered in the tragic and regrettable loss of life occasioned by the disaster to the * Empress of Ireland.' At the same time we beg your Royal Highness to accept the assurance of our personal sympathy for the sad event which has spread sorrow in the land we are beholden to for the most generous hospitality.
(Sgd) Emilio Rabasa.
(Sgd) Augustin Rodrigues.
(Sgd) Louis Elguero.
Consulado General de la Republica Argentina.
Carleton Chambers, 74 Sparks Street,
Ottawa, Canada,
June 2nd, 1914.
Sir,-In the absence of the Consul General, Mr. Carlos A Galarce, and in the name of the

Argentine Government, I wish to show you my deepest sympathy in the appalling disaster to the steamer Empress of Ireland, in wThich many Canadian lives were lost.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
D. Saavedrat,
In-charge.
To the Right Honourable R. L. Borden, P.C., Ottawa City.
On motion of Mr. Borden, the House adjourned at 12.20 a.m. Friday.
